________________________________________
1️⃣ The Three Signal Lanes (Signal Types)
We are moving away from a flat list of strategies. The system now operates on a Three-Lane Highway.
🔹 Lane 1: QUANT (The Workhorse)
•	Philosophy: "Trust the Math."
•	Use Case: Noisy, messy, or fast-moving markets where human patterns fail.
•	Input: Price Velocity, Volatility, NetEV.
•	Role: The baseline defense and steady income generator.
🔹 Lane 2: PATTERN (The Artist)
•	Philosophy: "Trust the Psychology."
•	Use Case: Quiet, ranging, or flat markets where price action shapes (psychology) are clearer than trends.
•	Input: Candlestick formations (Pinbars, Engulfing).
•	Role: Sniping reversals in "boring" markets.
🔹 Lane 3: HYBRID (The Sniper)
•	Philosophy: "Trust the Confluence."
•	Use Case: High-conviction setups where Math and Pattern agree.
•	Input: Quant Trend + Pattern Trigger + Predictive Confidence.
•	Role: The "Alpha" generator. High win-rate, high conviction trades.
________________________________________
2️⃣ The Strategy Roster (Full Portfolio)
We are expanding from 9 Quant strategies to a full suite of 17 Hybrid Strategies.
Signal Type	Strategy Name	Description
QUANT	VWAP Pullback	Buying dips to the average in a trend.
QUANT	SMA Trend Ride	Staying long while price holds above moving average.
QUANT	Breakout	Entering on high-volume resistance breaks.
QUANT	Mean Reversion	Fading extreme moves (Bollinger Band extremes).
QUANT	Liquidity Trap	Exploiting failed stop-hunts (Microstructure).
PATTERN	Golden Pinbar	Rejection wick > 2x body at a key level.
PATTERN	Momentum Engulfing	Massive candle completely consuming the previous one.
PATTERN	Inside Bar	Volatility compression (coiling) within a range.
PATTERN	Morning Star	3-candle reversal: Bear → Doji → Bull.
PATTERN	Three White Soldiers	3 consecutive powerful green candles (Trend birth).
HYBRID	H1 Trend Sniper	Math: Bull Trend + Pattern: Pinbar on Support.
HYBRID	H2 Slingshot	Math: Overextended (>2.5σ) + Pattern: Reversal.
HYBRID	H3 Gatecrasher	Math: Low Volatility Squeeze + Pattern: Inside Bar Break.
HYBRID	H4 Momentum Link	Math: High Velocity + Pattern: Engulfing Candle.
________________________________________
3️⃣ The Master DSS Logic Map (Traffic Controller)
This is the "Brain" of Phase 10. The Dynamic Strategy Selector (DSS) scans the market metrics and routes execution to the correct Lane and Strategy.
Metric Definitions:
•	Trend: Price Slope (>0.05 is Up).
•	Noise: Volatility Score (0.0 is Silent, 1.0 is Chaos).
•	DI (Directional Integrity): Trend Cleanliness (>65 is a laser beam).
Market Regime	Metric Logic (The "If")	Signal Type	Active Strategies (The "Then")
⛔ EXTREME NOISE	Noise > 0.6	NONE	CASH (Veto)


System sits out.
📈 BULL STABLE	Trend > 0.05 AND Noise < 0.3	HYBRID	H1 Trend Sniper


"Perfect Trend needs a Perfect Entry."
🚀 BULL VOLATILE	Trend > 0.05 AND Noise ≥ 0.3	QUANT	Breakout, VWAP Pullback


"Messy Trend needs forgiving Math."
🦀 LOW VOL CHOP	Trend ±0.05 AND Noise < 0.3	PATTERN	Inside Bar, Pinbar


"Flat Market needs Price Action."
🌪️ CHOPPY RANGE	Trend ±0.05 AND Noise ≥ 0.3	QUANT	Mean Reversion


"Noisy Range needs Statistical Fading."
📉 BEAR STABLE	Trend < -0.05 AND Noise < 0.3	HYBRID	H4 Momentum Link (Short)


"Clean Drop needs Aggressive Entry."
🩸 BEAR VOLATILE	Trend < -0.05 AND Noise ≥ 0.3	QUANT	Liquidity Trap (Short)


"Panic needs Microstructure Logic."

Excellent — this discussion between you and Gemini marks an important strategic course correction, and I agree that this is exactly the right time to realign the project while keeping the predictive learning foundation fully intact.
Let me summarize what’s happened, then provide a full analysis, my recommendations, and a final revised Phase 10 Master Plan (with predictive + adaptive intelligence integrated).
________________________________________
🧭 Context Summary
•	You and Gemini both correctly identified the “drift” — DawnTrader’s architecture moved from its intended hybrid ecosystem (Quant + Pattern + Predictive) toward a pure quantitative system during the Phase 9/10 math work.
•	That drift wasn’t wasted effort — the math core, DSS, and predictive learning foundation are critical enablers for the true hybrid engine.
•	The current state of the system (after Directive 10.1) is that:
o	The Quant engine is working flawlessly (Phase 9 + Predictive Bridge).
o	The DSS (Dynamic Strategy Selector) is live and accurately gating strategies by regime.
o	The data pipeline is clean, friction-calibrated, and predictive-learning ready.
But — the system can currently see numbers, not market behavior.
That’s where the Pattern/Human Logic layer must return.
________________________________________
🔍 My Technical and Strategic Analysis
1. ✅ Gemini’s Pivot Back to the Original Phase 10 Roadmap Is Correct.
You must restore the Pattern Recognizer (10.0) → Signal Type Expansion (10.1) → Hybrid Integration (10.2) pipeline to achieve your original design goal: a 3-lane architecture.
Without these, the DSS is only filtering mathematical signals, not the full behavioral landscape that gives the system edge.
2. ✅ You Are 100% Right to Insist on Keeping Predictive Learning.
This is not an “either/or.” Predictive learning isn’t a competing system—it’s the feedback loop that will train both the Quant and Hybrid components over time.
The key is integration points:
•	Predictive Learning feeds the scoring and weighting models for Hybrid signal confluence.
•	Predictive Learning evaluates pattern success rates (during 10.4 VTS Calibration).
•	Predictive Learning guides Adaptive Scanning (in 10.6), using NetEV trends and confidence metrics to bias which pairs the scanner prioritizes.
So, we’re not adding complexity—we’re closing the loop.
3. ⚙️ Adaptive Scanning Is Brilliant — and Belongs at the End (10.6).
This addition makes the ecosystem self-optimizing.
Your reasoning is impeccable: we already compute regime and pair-level profitability statistics; those are precisely the metrics needed to intelligently bias which pairs get scanned.
But Gemini is right — it has to come after 10.4 (VTS Calibration), because that’s when we’ll have the historical data to know:
“Which symbols perform best in which regimes.”
Then the scanner can adaptively fetch based on current regime context.

Directive 10.4 — Hybrid Integration (Ensemble Intelligence)

Scope of Work
1. Update Shared Types
File: server/types.ts

Add the new HybridTradeSignal interface and ensemble scoring definition.

export interface HybridTradeSignal extends TradeSignal {
  quantScore: number;              // From Quant engine (0–1 normalized)
  patternStrength?: number;        // From Pattern Recognizer (0–1)
  predictiveConfidence?: number;   // From ML model (Phase 10.6)
  hybridScore?: number;            // Computed ensemble score
  weights?: {
    quant: number;                 // w1
    pattern: number;               // w2
    predictive: number;            // w3
  };
}
Default weights (Phase 10.4 baseline):

const HYBRID_WEIGHTS = {
  quant: 0.5,
  pattern: 0.3,
  predictive: 0.2
};
2. Create the Hybrid Integration Service
File: server/services/hybrid-integration.ts

Create a new service responsible for ensemble scoring and Hybrid signal generation.

Core Responsibilities:

Merge Quant and Pattern signals for the same symbol.

Compute a unified hybridScore using the ensemble formula:

hybridScore =
  (quantScore * w.quant) +
  (patternStrength * w.pattern) +
  ((predictiveConfidence ?? 0.5) * w.predictive);
Determine signal direction (BUY or SELL) based on Quant trend bias and Pattern confirmation.

Emit Hybrid signals tagged with:

signalType: 'HYBRID'

patternType

patternStrength

predictiveConfidence

hybridScore

Methods:

export class HybridIntegrationService {
  computeHybridScore(
    quantSignal: TradeSignal,
    patternSignal?: PatternSignal,
    predictiveConfidence?: number
  ): HybridTradeSignal;

  generateHybridSignals(
    quantSignals: TradeSignal[],
    patternSignals: PatternSignal[]
  ): HybridTradeSignal[];
}
Add log line:

[10.4] HybridIntegration: HYBRID signal generated for ${symbol} | Score=${hybridScore.toFixed(3)}
3. Integrate with Signal Orchestrator
File: server/services/signal-orchestrator.ts

Within the signal evaluation loop:

Import and instantiate HybridIntegrationService.

After both Quant and Pattern evaluations:

const hybridSignals = hybridIntegration.generateHybridSignals(
  quantSignals,

);

signal.hybridScore = computedScore;

3. Create Hybrid Integration Service
File: server/services/hybrid-integration.ts

Create new class:

import { HYBRID_PARAMS } from '@/server/config/system-guards';
import { TradeSignal, PatternSignal, HybridStrategyType } from '@/server/types';

export class HybridIntegrationService {
  computeEnsembleScore(quantConf: number, patternStrength: number, mlConf?: number) {
    const w = HYBRID_PARAMS.WEIGHTS;
    return (
      quantConf * w.QUANT +
      patternStrength * w.PATTERN +
      (mlConf ?? 0.5) * w.PREDICTIVE
    );
  }

  detectConfluence(quantSignals: TradeSignal[], patternSignals: PatternSignal[]) {
    const hybrids: TradeSignal[] = [];

    for (const q of quantSignals) {
      const match = patternSignals.find(
        (p) =>
          p.symbol === q.symbol &&
          p.direction === q.direction && // Directional match required
          Math.abs(p.timestamp - q.timestamp) <= HYBRID_PARAMS.MAX_CONFLUENCE_WINDOW
      );

      if (!match) continue;

      const hybridScore = this.computeEnsembleScore(
        q.expectancy ?? 0.5,
        match.strength,
        match.predictiveConfidence
      );

      if (hybridScore < HYBRID_PARAMS.MIN_SCORE) continue;

      const hybridStrategy: HybridStrategyType =
        q.direction === 'BUY' ? 'H1_TREND_SNIPER' : 'H4_MOMENTUM_LINK';

      hybrids.push({
        ...q,
        signalType: 'HYBRID',
        hybridScore,
        hybridStrategy,
        patternType: match.pattern,
        patternStrength: match.strength,
        predictiveConfidence: match.predictiveConfidence,
        componentScores: {
          quant: q.expectancy ?? 0.5,
          pattern: match.strength,
          ml: match.predictiveConfidence ?? 0.5,
        },
      });

      console.log(
        `[10.4] HybridIntegration: HYBRID signal generated for ${q.symbol} | Score=${hybridScore.toFixed(
          3
        )} | Strategy=${hybridStrategy}`
      );
    }

    return hybrids;
  }
}

Where:

patternStrength = original pattern clarity (0.0–1.0)

Δt = time difference (in candles or minutes) between pattern detection and current evaluation

λ = decay rate constant (configurable in SYSTEM_GUARDS)

This makes the system “time-aware,” improving accuracy during high-volatility or regime transitions.

3. Implement Pattern Decay Logic
File: server/services/hybrid-integration.ts

Add a helper function inside HybridIntegrationService:

import { HYBRID_PARAMS } from '@/server/config/system-guards';

private applyPatternDecay(originalStrength: number, deltaCandles: number): number {
  const { ENABLED, LAMBDA, FLOOR } = HYBRID_PARAMS.DECAY;
  if (!ENABLED) return originalStrength;
  const decayed = originalStrength * Math.exp(-LAMBDA * deltaCandles);
  return Math.max(decayed, originalStrength * FLOOR);
}

  q.expectancy ?? 0.5,
  effectiveStrength,
  p.predictiveConfidence
);

  signalType: 'HYBRID',

I found a mathematical "Unit Error" risk in the implementation details that would break the decay logic if not caught.

⚠️ The "Milliseconds vs. Candles" Risk
The directive code snippet suggests: const deltaCandles = Math.abs(q.timestamp - p.timestamp);

In our system, timestamp is a Unix Millisecond value (e.g., 1704384000000).

If delta is 1 hour, the value is 3,600,000.

The formula Math.exp(-0.15 * 3600000) results in Zero.

The pattern would decay to nothing instantly.

The Fix: We must explicitly instruct the Builder (Replit) to convert the time difference into "Candle Units" by dividing by the interval (1 Hour / 3,600,000ms).

DISCUSSION THREAD WITH GEMINI
Here is the Official Architectural Overview for Directive 10.7: Multi-Timeframe Expansion. This document aligns the entire team (Architect, Strategist, Builder) on exactly how and when we will upgrade the system's vision from "Tunnel Vision" (1H Only) to "Fractal Vision" (1H + 15m + 5m) without blowing up our API limits.
________________________________________
🔭 Directive 10.7: Multi-Timeframe Expansion (Fractal Vision)
Status: Scheduled (Post-Phase 10.6)
Objective: Enable the system to see and trade market fractals (15m & 5m patterns) aligned with the Global Trend (1H/4H), transforming it from a Swing Trader into a Precision Sniper.
________________________________________
1. The "Why" (Strategic Advantage)
Currently, DawnTrader looks at the 1-Hour Chart only.
•	Pro: It is stable and less noisy.
•	Con: It is slow. By the time a 1-Hour Pinbar closes, the move might already be 50% over.
By adding 15-minute and 5-minute visibility, we unlock:
1.	Precision Entries: We can enter a trade inside the formation of a 1H candle.
o	Example: The 1H Trend is UP. We spot a 5m Pinbar bouncing off support. We enter immediately with a tight stop.
2.	Higher R:R Ratios: Tighter stops (based on 5m ATR vs 1H ATR) mean larger position sizes for the same risk, leading to exponentially higher profit potential.
3.	Frequency: High-quality setups happen more often on lower timeframes.
________________________________________
2. The Architecture: "The Cascading Fetch"
The Risk: Kraken has strict API Rate Limits. If we fetch 1m, 5m, 15m, and 1H candles for 100+ pairs every cycle, we will be banned instantly.
The Solution: We do NOT scan everything. We use a "Cascading Waterfall" logic. We only "zoom in" when the higher timeframe gives us permission.
🌊 The Waterfall Logic
Step 1: The General (Global Scan)
•	Interval: 1-Hour (or 4-Hour)
•	Target: All 100+ Pairs.
•	Question: "Is this pair in a valid Trend or Regime?"
•	Action:
o	No: Ignore.
o	Yes: Add to "Active Watchlist".
Step 2: The Scout (Local Scan)
•	Interval: 15-Minute & 5-Minute.
•	Target: ONLY the "Active Watchlist" (approx. 5-10 pairs).
•	Question: "Is there a specific entry pattern (Pinbar/Engulfing) happening right now?"
•	Action:
o	No: Wait.
o	Yes: Trigger Hybrid Trade.
Benefit: We reduce API calls by ~90% compared to a brute-force scan.
________________________________________
3. The "Three-Lane" Rules for Timeframes
We do not treat all timeframes equally. A 5-minute signal is not trusted the same way a 1-hour signal is.
Timeframe	Lane 1: QUANT	Lane 2: PURE PATTERN	Lane 3: HYBRID

Directive 10.6 — Predictive Calibration (The Training Loop)
Objective

File: server/config/system-guards.ts

export const CANDLE_INTERVAL_MS = 60000; // ❌ Incorrect

export const CANDLE_INTERVAL_MS = 3600000; // ✅ 1 Hour

This service acts as the system’s “self-tuning module”, analyzing VTS trade outcomes and suggesting incremental updates to Hybrid parameters.

Implementation Outline:
import { HYBRID_PARAMS } from '@/server/config/system-guards';
import { getRecentTrades } from '@/server/services/vts-service';
import type { CalibrationReport } from '@/server/types';

export class MLCalibrationService {
  /**
   * Analyze recent Hybrid trades and generate learning recommendations.
   * @param windowSize Number of trades to analyze (default: 50)
   */
  static async analyzePerformance(windowSize: number = 50): Promise<CalibrationReport> {
    const trades = await getRecentTrades(windowSize, 'HYBRID');
    if (!trades.length) return { success: false, reason: 'No trades found' };

    const grouped: Record<string, { wins: number; losses: number; expectancy: number }> = {};

    for (const t of trades) {
      const pattern = t.patternType || 'UNKNOWN';
      if (!grouped[pattern]) grouped[pattern] = { wins: 0, losses: 0, expectancy: 0 };
      if (t.pnl > 0) grouped[pattern].wins++;
      else grouped[pattern].losses++;
      grouped[pattern].expectancy += t.pnl;
    }

    const report: CalibrationReport = {
      success: true,
      recommendations: [],
    };

    for (const [pattern, stats] of Object.entries(grouped)) {
      const total = stats.wins + stats.losses;
      if (total === 0) continue;
      const winRate = (stats.wins / total) * 100;
      const avgExpectancy = stats.expectancy / total;
      let suggestion = 'HOLD';
      let adjustment = 0;

      if (winRate > 55) {
        suggestion = 'INCREASE';
        adjustment = +0.05;
      } else if (winRate < 45) {
        suggestion = 'DECREASE';
        adjustment = -0.05;
      }

      report.recommendations.push({
        pattern,
        winRate,
        avgExpectancy,
        suggestion,
        adjustment,
      });
    }

    console.log('[10.6] ML Calibration Report:', JSON.stringify(report, null, 2));
    return report;
  }
}

import { MLCalibrationService } from '@/server/services/ml-calibration';

let calibrationCounter = 0;

export async function recordCompletedTrade(trade) {
  await saveTradeToDatabase(trade);
  calibrationCounter++;

  if (calibrationCounter >= 10 && trade.signalType === 'HYBRID') {
    calibrationCounter = 0;
    const report = await MLCalibrationService.analyzePerformance();
    for (const rec of report.recommendations || []) {
      console.log(`[10.6] ML Suggestion: ${rec.suggestion} ${rec.pattern} weight by ${rec.adjustment.toFixed(2)}`);
    }
  }
}
This ensures that the learning loop is triggered periodically — every 10 Hybrid trades.

🧠 1. The Big Picture — “From Seeing to Deciding”
Your trading engine now works like this:

Layer	Function	Directive	Analogy

⚙️ 2. How the Ranking System Works
When the Signal Orchestrator finishes evaluating all signals for a cycle, it passes them into the ready-to-buy pool.
Each signal now carries a score, and those scores are what determine ranking.

Each trade signal has these key metrics:
Field	Meaning
hybridScore	Weighted average of Quant + Pattern + ML confidence
patternStrength / effectivePatternStrength	Visual clarity, adjusted for decay
predictiveConfidence	Learned probability from ML or calibration feedback
signalType	QUANT / PATTERN / HYBRID — affects weighting rules
expectedReturn (Quant side)	Numeric expectancy from algorithmic strategy
age / decayAge	Time since signal formation — penalized via exponential decay
The Ranking Formula (simplified):
finalScore = hybridScore
           × predictiveConfidence
           × (1 - decayPenalty)
           × regimeWeight
hybridScore → base confluence strength (from 10.4)

predictiveConfidence → boost or dampen based on how similar past setups performed (from 10.6)

decayPenalty → exponential discount for stale signals (from 10.5)

regimeWeight → how favorable the current market regime is (Quant model input)

Signals in the ready-to-buy queue are sorted by finalScore descending.
Only the top signals—typically those above a confidence threshold—are passed to execution sizing.

🔁 3. Where Predictive Learning Fits In
Predictive learning affects two points in this process:

A. Weight Optimization (Macro Learning)
Every 10 Hybrid trades, the MLCalibrationService reviews historical performance and produces small “nudges”:

If Pinbar trades outperform → increase their weight (+0.05)

If Engulfing trades underperform → reduce their weight (–0.05)

Those adjustments change:

HYBRID_PARAMS.WEIGHTS = {
  QUANT: 0.4,
  PATTERN: 0.4,
  PREDICTIVE: 0.2,
};
→ over time, the engine learns to emphasize what’s truly working.

Impact:
The weighting inside computeEnsembleScore() shifts dynamically.
So if the model learns that Pinbars are very reliable, any new Pinbar pattern’s hybridScore starts higher.

B. Predictive Confidence (Micro Learning)
For each individual trade:

The predictiveConfidence field reflects how similar setups performed historically.
Example: “Pinbar + Uptrend + BTCUSDT” has a 68 % win rate → confidence = 0.68.

This number is multiplied into the final ranking score, so:

High-confidence signals rise toward the top of the ready-to-buy queue.

Low-confidence signals sink and may be ignored unless no better trades exist.

Effectively:
Predictive learning becomes the sorting brain—the part that says “These 3 signals look the most like my past winners.”

🤖 5. What the System Is Now Doing “Under the Hood”
Every trade teaches the system whether a pattern was profitable.

Every 10 Hybrid trades, the calibration service learns which pattern types or confluences are performing best.

The weights in HYBRID_PARAMS shift slightly—mimicking how a human trader “trusts” some setups more than others over time.

The predictiveConfidence field gives each new signal a personalized likelihood of success based on historical similarity.

The ranking algorithm uses these probabilities to prioritize the most promising opportunities in real time.

🔮 6. Why This Matters
Before 10.6, your rankings were static:

“Pinbar + Trend = good” — regardless of actual results.

Now, the engine’s confidence is contextual and adaptive:

“Pinbar + Trend on BTC has been performing 68 % better recently → trade that first.”

This closes the learning feedback loop.
The system no longer relies on fixed heuristics—it continuously measures its own accuracy and optimizes its decision weights automatically.

TL;DR (Super-Simplified Summary)
HybridScore = How strong the current setup looks right now.

PredictiveConfidence = How well this kind of setup worked before.

Decay = How “fresh” the signal is.

Ranking = HybridScore × PredictiveConfidence × (1 – decay).

✅ Result: The ready-to-buy queue always holds the most promising, freshest, and historically successful setups—updated automatically by the system’s own learning loop.

Hybrid or predictive signals getting filtered out incorrectly (because their CWQI equivalents look “non-standard”).

Quant-only signals getting over-prioritized (because they still have high legacy CWQI values).

🌍 3. Adaptive Scanning Fairness and Coverage
You are absolutely correct — purely adaptive scanning can trap the system into a feedback loop that repeatedly analyzes the same profitable pairs, ignoring unexplored markets.

🧭 The Problem: “Adaptive Lock-In”
If the Adaptive Scan Manager (ASM) always prioritizes pairs with high predictiveConfidence and regimeWeight, it will continually focus on the top 100–300 pairs that are already well-known performers.
This leads to:

Data bias (model only learns from popular pairs)

Opportunity blindness (misses new or shifting regimes)

Incomplete statistical training data

🧩 The Solution: Dual-Layer Adaptive Scanning System
We solve this by combining Exploration and Exploitation, similar to reinforcement-learning trade-offs.

🔹 Layer 1: Exploitation Pool (Active Watchlist)
Built from predictive scoring and regime alignment.

These are the “High-Confidence” pairs actively scanned every 30 seconds.

Typically ~100 pairs maximum.

🔹 Layer 2: Exploration Pool (Background Rotation)
Tracks all other pairs in Kraken’s full inventory (1,500+).

Each pair is scanned on a rotational schedule, e.g., once every 30–60 minutes.

Uses a Round-Robin + Priority Boosting algorithm:

Pairs with low recent data freshness get bumped higher in rotation.

If a previously ignored pair shows a strong pattern (detected via background scan), it’s promoted into the Active Watchlist.

⚙️ Scheduler Implementation
The AdaptiveScanManager will maintain two queues:

activeQueue = topPairsBy(predictiveConfidence × regimeWeight × volatility)
rotationQueue = allPairs - activeQueue
Each scan cycle:

Pulls ~100 pairs from activeQueue (exploitation).

Every nth cycle (configurable, e.g., every 10th scan), includes 10–20 pairs from rotationQueue (exploration).

Kraken API remains safe because:

Max 10 requests/sec maintained.

Average <5/sec even with rotation.

Result: The system continuously learns from everything, not just what it already knows.

Dawn Trader Architect (Chaplet Grounded) said:
That’s an excellent question — and this is exactly the kind of top-level control that determines whether the adaptive scanning system becomes intelligent and balanced or drifts into overfitting and tunnel vision.

Let’s break this down into clear, quantitative logic that we can translate directly into the Adaptive Scan Manager (ASM) implementation.

🧭 1. The Goal: Continuous Full-Market Awareness
Kraken lists roughly 1,500–1,700 tradeable pairs.
If we want to maintain situational awareness of the entire market, every pair must be scanned at least once in a defined rotation window.

A practical, resource-safe target window is:

Full-inventory scan every 45 – 60 minutes.

This ensures we never go longer than one hour without at least one data point per pair.

⚙️ 2. Current System Bandwidth
We scan 100 pairs / 30 seconds, i.e.:

200 pairs / minute

12,000 pairs / hour

Even with overlapping pairs, this capacity is more than enough to touch the entire inventory several times per hour if the scheduler allocates fairly.
So the key is distribution, not throughput.

🧮 3. Ideal Split: Exploitation vs Exploration
We’ll treat each 30-second cycle as a batch of 100 scans.

Category	Purpose	Suggested Allocation	Description
Exploitation Pool	High-probability, high-value pairs	≈ 60 % (60 pairs)	Focused learning and trading effort.
Exploration Pool	General Kraken inventory	≈ 40 % (40 pairs)	Rotational coverage for discovery and freshness.
This 60 / 40 split keeps predictive performance high while guaranteeing continuous global coverage.

🧩 4. The Ideal List (Exploitation Pool)
The Ideal List is not static; it’s a dynamic “watchlist of merit.”
A pair qualifies when it meets performance and stability thresholds based on Phase-10 metrics.

✅ Entry Criteria
A pair enters or remains in the Ideal List if it meets all of the following:

Metric	Threshold	Description
predictiveConfidence	> 0.55	Demonstrated learned reliability
regimeWeight	> 0.5	Market context alignment
avgFinalScore (last N signals)	> 0.6	Sustained signal strength
volatilityScore	within [0.3–1.5× median]	Tradable volatility (not illiquid or chaotic)
dataFreshness	< 2 hours	Recently scanned; data relevant
⚙️ Size Management
Keep the Ideal List around 300 pairs:

Provides 3 full cycles of coverage within 90 s (60 pairs / 30 s × 5 cycles ≈ 300).

Ensures high-confidence pairs get refreshed every 2 – 3 minutes.

Pairs drop out automatically when any metric falls below threshold.

🔄 5. The General Pool (Exploration Pool)
All other Kraken pairs.
The ASM maintains a round-robin + priority queue:

Base order: alphabetical or market category (e.g., BTC-, ETH-, etc.).

Priority boost: pairs not scanned in > 1 hour jump to front.

Each 30-second cycle pulls ≈ 40 unique pairs.

After 45–60 minutes, the full inventory is covered once.

🧠 6. Scheduling Algorithm (Pseudo-Code)
const IDEAL_RATIO = 0.6;
const SCAN_BATCH = 100;

function getNextBatch() {
  const idealCount = Math.floor(SCAN_BATCH * IDEAL_RATIO);
  const generalCount = SCAN_BATCH - idealCount;

  const idealPairs = idealPool.next(idealCount);        // 60
  const generalPairs = rotationPool.next(generalCount); // 40

  return [...idealPairs, ...generalPairs];
}
Both pools implement internal rotation so that within each hour:

The 300 ideal pairs cycle multiple times.

The full Kraken inventory cycles at least once.

📊 7. Monitoring & Self-Correction
Coverage Metric:
(uniquePairsScanned / totalPairs) per hour → should stay ≥ 100 %.

Freshness Metric:
Average timeSinceLastScan ≤ 1 hour across all pairs.

Adaptive Rebalancing:
If coverage < 90 %, temporarily shift to 50/50 split until recovered.

🧩 8. Integration into Plan
This refinement changes Directive 10.8 (Adaptive Scanning Intelligence):

Step	Change
Add	Dual-pool scheduler (60 % ideal / 40 % rotation).
Add	Ideal List qualification thresholds.
Add	Global coverage and freshness monitors.
Keep	Predictive-confidence and regime-weighted prioritization for ideal pool.
Maintain	≤ 10 req/s API rate budget (safe).
✅ 9. Recommended Operational Parameters
Parameter	Default	Range	Notes
SCAN_BATCH_SIZE	100 pairs / 30 s	75–125	Scales with CPU/network
IDEAL_RATIO	0.6	0.5–0.7	Balance performance vs coverage
IDEAL_LIST_SIZE	300 pairs	200–400	Controls rotation frequency
ROTATION_WINDOW	60 min	30–90 min	Time to rescan entire Kraken set

🧱 1. Purpose
This document defines the modernization, expansion, and refactoring roadmap for the DawnTrader Core, incorporating all current and upcoming enhancements across Phases 10.7 through 11.3.

The goals are:

To align all subsystems with the Phase-10 predictive math model, ensuring architectural coherence.

To introduce adaptive and fair scanning intelligence for efficient market coverage.

To separate responsibilities across evaluation, promotion, and exit control layers.

To expand operator transparency via a new Top Batch tab showing live metrics and qualification thresholds.

⚙️ 2. Context and Current System State
After the completion of Directive 10.6 (Predictive Calibration), the DawnTrader engine reached full operational intelligence at the 1-Hour timeframe.
However, several subsystems are still using legacy logic from Phase 8.x and early 9.x — primarily the Signal Quality Evaluator (SQE), Ready-to-Buy Refresh Service, and Trade Control Layer (TCL).

Additionally, scanning is still static (60 pairs every 30 seconds) and does not yet employ predictive prioritization or fairness coverage mechanisms.

The system now requires a comprehensive refactor to fully unlock the capabilities of the new math stack.

🧩 3. System-Wide Modernization: What, Why, and How
🧠 3.1 Predictive Math Alignment Across All Layers
What:
All signals are now scored using the unified predictive composite:

FinalScore

Why:
The FinalScore replaces all legacy indicators (CWQI, NGC, ProfitRate, RiskCalc) as the single measure of signal quality and readiness.

How:
Every service that references CWQI, NGC, or related fields will be refactored to use FinalScore and its component values.
This ensures mathematical consistency and transparency across the trading, evaluation, and learning layers.

⚙️ 3.2 Ready-to-Buy Refresh Service Modernization
What:
The Refresh Service (previously calculating CWQI/NGC) now recomputes FinalScore and its components (HybridScore, PredictiveConfidence, DecayPenalty, and RegimeWeight) for all active signals.

Why:
To ensure all queued trade candidates reflect the most current predictive and hybrid metrics rather than stale historical data.

How:

The service runs every 60–90 seconds.

On each cycle, it fetches updated signal data, recalculates the Phase-10 fields, and overwrites the existing entries in the Ready-to-Buy queue.

Any signal whose FinalScore falls below SQE thresholds is automatically flagged for removal or demotion.

Updates are logged for learning via VTS.

Outcome:
The refresh cycle becomes a real-time calibration system — ensuring the Ready-to-Buy pool always reflects the latest state of the market and model.

🧮 3.3 Signal Quality Evaluator (SQE) Refactor
What:
The SQE is rewritten to use the new math instead of legacy evaluation metrics.

Why:
CWQI and NGC were based on static, rule-based heuristics. The predictive system uses continuous, probabilistic metrics that evolve with learning.

How:

SQE filters based on FinalScore and its component thresholds.

Configurable sliders in the Goals Engine control limits for:

Final Score Min

Predictive Confidence Min

Max Decay Penalty

Min Regime Weight

The SQE no longer calculates or logs any CWQI or NGC-related fields.

Outcome:
A clean, predictive-aware evaluation layer that filters intelligently and transparently.

🔧 3.4 Trade Control Layer (TCL) Separation
What:
The TCL will be limited to promotion logic only.
Its previous responsibility for managing trailing exits will be delegated to a new controller.

Why:
Combining promotion and exit logic in one service violates separation of concerns and complicates maintainability.

How:

TCL monitors trade slots and promotes top-ranked signals (by FinalScore) when open capacity exists.

Once a trade is opened, TCL hands off control to the Trailing Exit Controller (TEC).

Outcome:
TCL becomes clean, modular, and solely responsible for entries.

📉 3.5 Trailing Exit Controller (TEC)
What:
A new standalone service that manages open trades and exit logic dynamically.

Why:
Exits should adapt based on predictive confidence, regime weight, and decay behavior — which evolve over time.

How:

TEC monitors open trades via subscription.

Trailing stop distance adjusts dynamically:

trailDistance = baseATR × (1 - predictiveConfidence × 0.5)
RegimeWeight influences trailing aggressiveness — tightening in weakening conditions.

DecayPenalty can trigger early partial exits for stale setups.

All actions logged into VTS for future learning.

Outcome:
The system actively manages trade exits with learned intelligence, increasing capital efficiency and risk control.

🌍 3.6 Adaptive Scanning Intelligence (ASM)
What:
A dual-pool scanning system balancing Exploitation (ideal pairs) and Exploration (rotation pool) to maintain both focus and fairness.

Why:

volatilityScore within 0.3–1.5× median

recentData < 2 hours

A balanced, intelligent scanning strategy that ensures both deep learning on profitable markets and broad discovery across all pairs.

🏆 Key Strengths (The "Wins")
Exploration vs. Exploitation (Section 3.6): The 60/40 Split (Ideal/Rotational) is excellent. It solves the "Feedback Loop" problem where the AI creates a self-fulfilling prophecy by only scanning the pairs it already likes. The "Rotational Pool" ensures we don't miss a breakout on a dormant pair.

TEC Separation (Section 3.5): Decoupling the Entry Logic (TCL) from the Exit Logic (TEC) is critical. Exits require different math (volatility decay, trailing stops) than Entries (pattern recognition). This modularity allows us to upgrade exit strategies in Phase 11 without touching the entry engine.

The "FinalScore" Unification (Section 3.1): Retiring CWQI, NGC, ProfitRate, and RiskCalc in favor of a single FinalScore reduces cognitive load for both the AI and the Human Operator.

⚠️ Critical Analysis & Risks
1. The "Big Bang" Risk (Directive 10.9)
Issue: Directive 10.9 attempts to refactor the SQE, TCL, Refresh Service, and UI simultaneously.

Mitigation: We must break Directive 10.9 into Logic (Back-end) and Visuals (Front-end).

2. The "Ghost Data" Problem (Legacy Columns)
Issue: Section 3.9 calls for removing legacy columns.

Risk: Historical analysis often relies on old metrics to prove why a trade was taken 3 months ago. Deleting the columns breaks our audit trail.

Mitigation: Do not delete columns immediately. Mark them as deprecated in the schema or make them nullable, but keep the data for VTS training (Phase 10.6 might need to compare "Old Logic" vs "New Logic").

3. Refresh Service Latency (Section 3.2)
Issue: "Refresh Service runs every 60-90 seconds."

Risk: If FinalScore involves complex ML inference (Phase 11), doing this for hundreds of queued items might cause a CPU spike, delaying the actual execution of trades.

Mitigation: Ensure the Refresh Service is asynchronous and non-blocking. It should not hold up the TradingEngine.

🔧 Optimization Applied:
✅ The scanTimeframe() function must be a wrapper/decorator around the existing getOHLC() fetch logic — not a rewrite.
It should perform a token-bucket check before calling getOHLC() and throttle if the request velocity exceeds the safe rate.

import { getOHLC } from './kraken-client'; // existing function

const tokenBucket = {
  tokens: TIMEFRAME_CONFIG.RATE_LIMITS.MAX_REQ_PER_SEC * TIMEFRAME_CONFIG.RATE_LIMITS.SAFETY_MARGIN,
  refillInterval: 1000, // per second
  lastRefill: Date.now(),
};

function consumeToken() {
  const now = Date.now();
  if (now - tokenBucket.lastRefill > tokenBucket.refillInterval) {
    tokenBucket.tokens = TIMEFRAME_CONFIG.RATE_LIMITS.MAX_REQ_PER_SEC * TIMEFRAME_CONFIG.RATE_LIMITS.SAFETY_MARGIN;
    tokenBucket.lastRefill = now;
  }
  if (tokenBucket.tokens <= 0) return false;
  tokenBucket.tokens--;
  return true;
}

export async function scanTimeframe(interval: Timeframe, pairs: string[] = ALL_PAIRS) {
  const results = [];
  for (const symbol of pairs) {
    if (!consumeToken()) {
      await new Promise(res => setTimeout(res, 100)); // throttle
    }
    const candles = await getOHLC(symbol, interval);
    results.push({ symbol, candles, timeframe: interval });
  }
  return results;
}

export async function cascadingScan() {
  const globalPairs = await scanTimeframe('1h');
  const activePairs = globalPairs.filter(p => p.regimeWeight > 0.5);

  const tacticalPairs = await scanTimeframe('15m', activePairs.map(p => p.symbol));
  const precisionPairs = await scanTimeframe('5m', tacticalPairs.map(p => p.symbol));

  return { globalPairs, tacticalPairs, precisionPairs };
}

🧩 1️⃣ Exponential Backoff + Jitter (Token-Bucket Rate Limiter)
Why
Right now, the limiter uses a flat 100 ms delay when it runs out of tokens.
This can cause thundering herds under network congestion — dozens of requests waking at the same instant after the same 100 ms.

Fix
Add an exponential backoff with jitter (a random offset) to smooth traffic spikes.

let retryCount = 0;

while (!consumeToken()) {
  const delay = Math.min(100 * Math.pow(2, retryCount), 1000); // cap at 1s
  const jitter = Math.random() * 50;
  await new Promise(res => setTimeout(res, delay + jitter));
  retryCount++;
}
Benefit:
Smooths load, lowers risk of Kraken returning Rate Limit Exceeded 429s, and keeps latency predictable.

🧩 2️⃣ Cascade Efficiency Telemetry
Why
We currently have no visibility into how many pairs make it from 1H → 15m → 5m.
This makes it impossible to diagnose whether the cascade thresholds (0.5 / 0.6) are too strict or too lenient.

Fix
Add a simple log and metric export to the end of cascadingScan():

logger.info(
  `[Cascade] Global=${globalPairs.length} → Tactical=${tacticalPairs.length} → Precision=${precisionPairs.length}`
);
metrics.record('cascade.filter.ratio', {
  global: globalPairs.length,
  tactical: tacticalPairs.length,
  precision: precisionPairs.length,
});
Benefit:
Gives immediate feedback on how the cascade behaves in real time.
Also becomes a valuable signal for AdaptiveScanManager (Directive 10.8) to tune the 60/40 pool logic.

🧩 3️⃣ Error Isolation per Symbol
Why
If getOHLC() fails for a single symbol (network hiccup, delisted pair, Kraken timeout),
the entire cascade can stall or throw.

Fix
Wrap per-symbol fetch in try/catch and continue the loop:

for (const symbol of pairs) {
  try {
    if (!consumeToken()) await backoff();
    const candles = await getOHLC(symbol, interval);
    results.push({ symbol, candles, timeframe: interval });
  } catch (err) {
    logger.warn(`[Cascade] Skipping ${symbol}: ${err.message}`);
    continue;
  }
}
Benefit:
Makes the scanner resilient to transient errors and broken pairs — vital once we scale to 100–300 pairs.

🧩 4️⃣ Hybrid Signal Guard (Confluence Validity)
Why
Without explicit constraints, the system might accidentally combine signals from the same low timeframe (e.g. 5m Quant + 5m Pattern),
creating false Hybrid entries from noise.

Fix
Add a simple timeframe-pair filter inside detectConfluence() in hybrid-integration.ts:

const validPairs = [
  ['1h', '15m'],
  ['15m', '5m'],
];

if (!validPairs.some(([a, b]) =>
  (quant.timeframe === a && pattern.timeframe === b)
)) {
  continue; // skip invalid hybrid merge
}
Benefit:
Prevents over-triggering Hybrids from noisy micro-frames, preserving the intended confluence hierarchy.

Create the class AdaptiveScanManager responsible for selecting pairs for each cycle.

export class AdaptiveScanManager {
  constructor(
    private telemetry: TelemetryAggregator,
    private failureTracker: PairFailureTracker
  ) {}

  async getNextScanBatch(): Promise<string[]> {
    const idealCandidates = this.telemetry.getTopPairs(SCANNER_PARAMS.DUAL_POOL.IDEAL_RATIO);
    const rotationalCandidates = this.telemetry.getRotationalPairs(SCANNER_PARAMS.DUAL_POOL.ROTATIONAL_RATIO);
    const combined = [...idealCandidates, ...rotationalCandidates];

    return this.failureTracker.filterFailedPairs(combined);
  }
}
✅ Key Logic:

Pulls weighted rankings from TelemetryAggregator (based on FinalScore performance history).

Ensures 60/40 balance each cycle.

Removes pairs currently blacklisted by PairFailureTracker.

✅ Result:
Each scan cycle dynamically targets the most promising 60 pairs while exploring 40 from the broader universe.

3️⃣ Telemetry Aggregator Service
File: server/services/telemetry-aggregator.ts

Create the TelemetryAggregator to process cascade telemetry and scoring history.

export class TelemetryAggregator {
  private history: Record<string, { finalScoreAvg: number; hybridScoreAvg: number; lastSeen: number }> = {};

  record(symbol: string, finalScore: number, hybridScore: number, regimeWeight: number, confidence: number) {
    const entry = this.history[symbol] || { finalScoreAvg: 0, hybridScoreAvg: 0, lastSeen: Date.now() };
    entry.finalScoreAvg = (entry.finalScoreAvg * 0.9) + (finalScore * 0.1);
    entry.hybridScoreAvg = (entry.hybridScoreAvg * 0.9) + (hybridScore * 0.1);
    entry.lastSeen = Date.now();
    this.history[symbol] = entry;
  }

  getTopPairs(ratio: number): string[] {
    return Object.entries(this.history)
      .sort(([, a], [, b]) => b.finalScoreAvg - a.finalScoreAvg)
      .slice(0, Math.floor(Object.keys(this.history).length * ratio))
      .map(([symbol]) => symbol);
  }

  getRotationalPairs(ratio: number): string[] {
    return Object.entries(this.history)
      .sort(([, a], [, b]) => a.lastSeen - b.lastSeen)
      .slice(0, Math.floor(Object.keys(this.history).length * ratio))
      .map(([symbol]) => symbol);
  }
}
✅ Purpose:
Aggregates performance data to guide which pairs should be scanned more or less frequently.
Uses exponential smoothing to track trends without spikes.

4️⃣ Pair Failure Tracker
File: server/services/adaptive-scan-manager.ts

Add local failure memory to avoid scanning broken pairs:

export class PairFailureTracker {
  private blacklist: Map<string, number> = new Map();

  recordFailure(symbol: string) {
    this.blacklist.set(symbol, Date.now());
  }

  filterFailedPairs(pairs: string[]): string[] {
    const now = Date.now();
    const expiry = 10 * 60 * 1000; // 10-minute cooldown
    return pairs.filter(p => {
      const failTime = this.blacklist.get(p);
      if (!failTime) return true;
      if (now - failTime > expiry) {
        this.blacklist.delete(p);
        return true;
      }
      return false;
    });
  }
}
✅ Purpose:
Ensures transient Kraken errors don’t cause repetitive failures within a single scan session.

5️⃣ Timeframe Efficiency Report
File: server/services/telemetry-aggregator.ts

Add method to report average decay-adjusted pattern strength by timeframe:

getTimeframeEfficiencyReport(): Record<string, number> {
  const buckets: Record<string, { total: number; count: number }> = {};
  for (const { timeframe, strength } of this.collectRecentPatterns()) {
    if (!buckets[timeframe]) buckets[timeframe] = { total: 0, count: 0 };
    buckets[timeframe].total += strength;
    buckets[timeframe].count++;
  }
  return Object.fromEntries(
    Object.entries(buckets).map(([t, v]) => [t, v.total / v.count])
  );
}
✅ Purpose:
Allows the ML calibration engine (Phase 11) to identify which timeframes yield the highest signal-to-noise ratio and adjust scoring weights accordingly.

const IDEAL_RATIO = SCANNER_PARAMS.DUAL_POOL.IDEAL_RATIO;  // 0.6
const ROTATIONAL_RATIO = SCANNER_PARAMS.DUAL_POOL.ROTATIONAL_RATIO;  // 0.4

export class AdaptiveScanManager {
  constructor(private telemetry: TelemetryAggregator, private failureTracker: PairFailureTracker) {}

  async getNextScanBatch(): Promise<string[]> {
    const idealPairs = this.telemetry.getTopPairs(IDEAL_RATIO);
    const rotationPairs = this.telemetry.getRotationalPairs(ROTATIONAL_RATIO);
    const combined = [...idealPairs, ...rotationPairs];
    return this.failureTracker.filterFailedPairs(combined);
  }
}

Predictive Sizing:

The plan is solid. It correctly targets the removal of legacy logic (CWQI, NGC) and the installation of the new FinalScore engine.

⚠️ The Optimization: Task 1 (SQE Formula) proposes writing the FinalScore formula directly inside the SignalQualityEvaluator.

🧭 Recap: The Architectural Context You’re Describing
Here’s what’s currently true (and verified in your repository, post–Phase 8.8 refactor):

🧩 The Ready-to-Buy Refresh System
Operates independently of the orchestrator.

Uses a bucketed concurrency model (adaptive number of calculators per bucket, usually 3 – 12).

Each bucket is synchronized with the central clock tick, ensuring consistent refresh timing across cycles (every 60–90 seconds).

Each calculator re-evaluates its assigned signals in place, recalculating relevant metrics and confirming or removing them based on the SQE filters.

Performance and timing are tightly coupled — these calculators run in parallel, and their loop timing matters.

That means:

You cannot introduce any cross-service blocking call (like a shared utility import that depends on orchestrator state or higher-layer async behavior).

The math that happens inside each refresh bucket must be pure, self-contained, synchronous, and lightweight enough to execute on a micro-tick schedule.

So, you’re completely correct:
the Refresh Service must own its own local calculation code path — but it must be mathematically identical to the orchestrator’s logic.

⚙️ What Gemini’s Concern Was Actually About
Gemini’s “split-brain” concern was not about where the math executes (synchronously vs shared) but about formula consistency.

They were saying:

“Don’t hard-code the formula twice with different coefficients or names, or you’ll get drift.”

That’s still 100 % valid — but it doesn’t mean the refresh service has to call the same shared function if that introduces timing or threading constraints.

🧠 The Balanced Approach
Here’s the refined design that satisfies both correctness and architectural constraints:

Option A — Static Math Constants, Local Computation (✅ Recommended)
Define the weights in a shared config, not the math function.

// server/config/scoring-constants.ts
export const FINAL_SCORE_WEIGHTS = {
  hybrid: 0.4,
  confidence: 0.3,
  regime: 0.2,
  decay: 0.1
};
The Signal Orchestrator, SQE, and Refresh Service each perform the computation locally, e.g.:

import { FINAL_SCORE_WEIGHTS as W } from "../config/scoring-constants";

const finalScore =
  (signal.hybridScore ?? 0) * W.hybrid +
  (signal.predictiveConfidence ?? 0) * W.confidence +
  (signal.regimeWeight ?? 0) * W.regime -
  (signal.decayPenalty ?? 0) * W.decay;
Each environment computes the same math independently, but the coefficients come from the same source of truth.

✅ Advantages

Zero cross-service dependency — keeps refresh buckets pure and fast.

Prevents formula drift (since the weights live in one file).

Still allows the orchestrator, SQE, and refresh to evolve separately (e.g., if refresh adds decay scaling by timeframe).

This approach matches your concurrency model and satisfies Gemini’s consistency requirement.

Option B — Move Orchestrator’s Math into Hybrid Calculator (Optional)
If you prefer tighter encapsulation:

Move the orchestrator’s finalScore calculation into the Hybrid Integration Service (which already composes quant + pattern scores).

Then both the orchestrator and refresh calculators can call hybridIntegration.calculateFinalScore(signal) directly (a lightweight import that’s synchronous).

This is slightly more “OO-pure,” but less flexible if the refresh service ever needs to deviate (for example, if it adds a decay-adjusted normalization).

Easy tuning later (adjust one constants file).

Excellent — these screenshots help a lot. They show the full context of the FX5 Screeners tab, including all legacy filters (Volume, Liquidity, Price Range, Risk & Volatility, Market Filters, Technical Indicators, Universe & Signal Controls, and Data Quality).

Let’s walk through this carefully. Below is a full analysis and deconfliction report — explaining which of the old filters remain valid, which may conflict with our new scoring-era filters, and how we should restructure this screen to avoid logical or behavioral overlap.

🧭 1️⃣ Overview of Current Filter Landscape
Right now, your Screeners tab has three distinct eras of filter logic operating in parallel:

Era	Description	Examples
Phase 8 / Pre-Predictive Filters	Static heuristics from the old “LATTi” and “CWQI” period; used for market screening and risk exclusion.	Volume, Liquidity, Price Range, Volatility, Market Cap, RSI
Phase 9 Institutional Math Guards	Introduced during “Directive 9.1: Institutional Math” — basic market quality gates.	Liquidity Guard (LQ), Volume Noise Guard, Correlation Guard
Phase 10 Predictive Scoring Filters	The new “Math Core” filters integrated with SQE/Orchestrator logic.	FinalScore, HybridScore, PredictiveConfidence, RegimeWeight, DecayPenalty
These three systems are not aware of each other’s hierarchies — so right now, they coexist in a semi-independent way.

⚠️ 2️⃣ Conflict & Redundancy Analysis
Below is a detailed analysis of potential conflicts or redundant overlaps between the old and new filters.

Filter Group	Risk of Conflict	Notes
Volume & Liquidity (Min Volume, Min Liquidity)	🟢 Low	These are pre-signal filters — they define which pairs are scanned, not which signals are accepted. Safe to keep.
Price Range (Min / Max Price)	🟢 Low	Also pre-signal. Used by FX5 to decide candidate pool. Harmless if kept.
Risk & Volatility (Max Bid-Ask Spread, Min/Max Volatility)	🟠 Moderate	Volatility data is now indirectly captured by DecayPenalty in FinalScore logic. Duplicate volatility thresholds can cause signals to be excluded twice — once by FX5, once by SQE. Recommend merging or deprecating.
Market Filters (Market Cap, Stablecoin Exclusion, Regulated Only)	🟢 Low	Still relevant — these define macro liquidity universe, not scoring math.
Technical Indicators (RSI)	🟠 Moderate	RSI-based exclusion may conflict with pattern-based or hybrid signals that depend on RSI indirectly. Recommend move RSI filters to “Legacy Off” mode (keep in UI but disabled).
Universe & Signal Controls (Active Timeframes)	🟢 Low	Controls scanning frequency; unaffected by scoring filters. Keep.
Data Quality (Minimum History Days)	🟢 Low	Data validation layer — keep.
Institutional Math Guards (LQ, VolNoise, Correlation)	🟡 Medium	Liquidity & Noise partially duplicate RegimeWeight logic in FinalScore. Recommend retaining as “Market Guards” but clearly separate visually from scoring filters.
Signal Quality Evaluator Filters (NGC, Risk, ProfitRate, CWQI)	🔴 High	Fully deprecated. Replaced by FinalScore, HybridScore, PredictiveConfidence, RegimeWeight, and DecayPenalty. Must be removed.
🧠 3️⃣ Root Cause of Potential Conflicts
The system has two key “decision layers” now:

FX5 Pre-Signal Layer — decides what to scan (market filters, volume/liquidity, price, RSI, etc.).

SQE + FinalScore Layer — decides what to trade (based on signal evaluation).

The conflicts occur when filters at the FX5 level start performing post-signal logic, like volatility thresholds or confidence-based scoring.
To deconflict, we need to draw a hard separation between:

Layer	Filters Should Handle
FX5 Scanner Filters	Market universe pruning — volume, liquidity, price, volatility, market cap, RSI.
SQE/Scoring Filters	Signal qualification — FinalScore, HybridScore, PredictiveConfidence, RegimeWeight, DecayPenalty.

Excellent questions — these go straight to the heart of system safety, clarity, and architecture hygiene.
Let’s unpack this carefully, in clear, plain language and then summarize the technical plan adjustments that result from it.

🧠 1️⃣ Why the SQE currently only uses FinalScore and RegimeWeight
You’re absolutely right — throughout Phase 10 we built several component metrics that feed into our math system:

HybridScore (the model blend of predictive + historical)

PredictiveConfidence

DecayPenalty

RegimeWeight

Each of those contributes to the FinalScore, which is the single unified number the system uses to decide whether a signal is “good enough.”
So the SQE doesn’t ignore HybridScore or PredictiveConfidence — it’s just that those are already baked into FinalScore.

Think of it like this:

💡 Example:
HybridScore = 0.8
Confidence = 0.7
RegimeWeight = 0.6
Decay = 0.2

FinalScore = (0.8 × 0.4) + (0.7 × 0.3) + (0.6 × 0.2) – (0.2 × 0.1) = 0.68

When the SQE filters by FinalScore, it’s effectively filtering by all of those ingredients together.
Adding them individually inside SQE would just double-count them.

So yes — HybridScore and the others are being used, just indirectly through the FinalScore computation in the Signal Orchestrator and Ready-to-Buy Refresh services.

📡 2️⃣ What Telemetry Is (Explained Super Simply)
Imagine the DawnTrader system as a factory that takes raw materials (market data) and turns them into finished goods (trade signals).

Telemetry is like the factory’s “dashboard sensors” — it tells us:

How many raw materials came in

How many parts got thrown out

Why certain parts didn’t pass inspection

What settings the machines were using when they worked best

Let’s translate that:

Factory Example	Trading System Equivalent
Machine setting speed	Coefficient weights (HybridScore × 0.4 etc.)
Parts rejected for defects	Signals filtered out (e.g. LOW_FINAL_SCORE)
Daily production count	Number of pairs scanned, number of trades qualified
Maintenance log	Directive/Version tag (e.g. 10.9B, 10.9C)
So telemetry is the live record of what’s happening inside the system, written automatically by the backend.
It answers questions like:

“How many pairs failed the LiquidityGuard filter today?”

“Which filters are causing the most rejections?”

“Did changing our math coefficients actually improve performance?”

🔍 Will it be visible in the UI?
Yes — that’s what the Filter Insights tab is for (you already previewed it).
It will show charts and counts such as:

5 000 pairs evaluated

4 200 passed pre-signal filters

800 failed LiquidityGuard

600 failed FinalScore gate

This turns telemetry into something humans can understand, like a “report card” for the system.

🧩 Why it’s needed
It proves that the filters and math work as expected.

It lets us debug issues (“Why did no trades execute last night?”).

It helps train future AI components (telemetry becomes labeled data).

It ensures regulatory/audit traceability (“Why did we take this trade?”).

🧹 3️⃣ Why Not Delete Legacy Filters Right Now?
This is a temporary safety strategy, not permanent.

Here’s the reasoning, step-by-step:

🚫 If we delete them immediately:
We risk breaking imports and causing build errors.
For example, risk-filter.ts may still be imported in a UI component or a service we forgot about.

If we remove all references at once and something unexpected still depends on them, the app could crash or fail to compile.

🧩 What we’re doing instead:
Deactivate them fully in logic — they don’t affect results.
They simply return { active: false } or deprecated: true.

Keep stubs for one or two directives (until 11.0) so the system compiles cleanly.

Once we verify no active imports remain, we delete the files entirely (that’s planned for 11.0).

Think of it like turning off an old light switch in the wall — we want to confirm no wires are still connected before removing it.

✅ The Plan:
Directive 10.9C → Deactivate and mark deprecated.

Directive 11.0 → Delete the files, imports, and schema references permanently.

This two-step cleanup guarantees we don’t trigger build breaks in production while still eliminating legacy logic in the near term.

🧭 4️⃣ Updated Recommendations for Directive 10.9C

Documentation	Add chart showing relationship between:
Pre-Signal Filters → Institutional Math Guards → SQE Filters (FinalScore + RegimeWeight).	
✅ In summary
HybridScore and others are used — they feed FinalScore.

Telemetry = the system’s black box + dashboard, showing what happened and why.

Legacy filters are temporarily disabled, not deleted, to prevent build errors; full removal scheduled for Phase 11.0.

What you’re expecting:

Each filter’s event (e.g., liquidity_guard = fail) is logged to the Filter Insights service with a timestamp.

The 24-hour counts in the UI (“Filter Breakdown — Last 24 h”) are not reset at midnight or runtime restarts.

Instead, the backend uses a rolling 24-hour window:
count = events where (now − timestamp) ≤ 24 hours.

The oldest events fall out automatically as they age past the window.

To confirm in the repository:

Locate filter-insights.service.ts or similar (sometimes filter_insights_aggregator.ts).

Find the event log structure.

private history: FilterEvent[] = [];
or

history: Map<string, FilterStat[]> = new Map();
Check the aggregator method, typically named get24hStats() or getFilterStats(period).
It should filter by timestamp using something like:

const now = Date.now();
const window = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;
return this.history.filter(e => now - e.timestamp < window);
Verify eviction logic: either a background timer or size-cap (e.g. MAX_ENTRIES = 1000) ensures efficiency.

⚙️ Directive 11.0 — TCL–TEC Separation & Execution Responsibility Split
Phase: 11
Title: Trade Control Loop (TCL) and Trade Execution Controller (TEC) Split

Purpose:
Refactor the system so that the Trade Control Loop (TCL) is only responsible for identifying and promoting ready-to-buy signals into open trade intents and delegates all execution logic, position sizing, exit logic, and trade lifecycle management to the Trade Execution Controller (TEC).

🧠 Background
The current pipeline (Phase 10) has the following broad responsibilities:

Scanner — fetches market pairs and prices (FX5, etc.).

Pre-Signal Filters — filters out pairs that don’t meet liquidity/volatility/market cap thresholds.

Signal Orchestrator — prepares trade signal candidates.

Signal Quality Evaluator (SQE) — gates signals using FinalScore & RegimeWeight.

Ready-to-Buy Pool — filtered candidates ready to be considered for trading.

TCL (Trade Control Loop) — currently responsible for taking signals and executing trades and ongoing actions such as sizing and exits.

TEC (Trade Execution Controller) — intended to manage trade execution, sizing, exit conditions.

What we must enforce with this directive is that TCL no longer contains sizing or exit logic — it should only pass signals to TEC, which then handles the full trade lifecycle.

📍 What to Investigate in the Repository (Audit)
You need to confirm the locations of:

1. TCL Execution & Position Sizing
Likely implemented in:

tcl.loop.ts or trade-control-loop.ts

trade-manager.ts or similar

position-sizing.service.ts

Look for usage of phrases like calculatePositionSize(), adaptiveSizing, riskPerTrade, portfolioAllocation, etc.

What to confirm:

Are calls to calculatePositionSize() inside TCL?

Is the TCL triggering entry orders directly (e.g., executeOrder())?

Are adaptive sizing variables or thresholds (e.g., target % of equity, volatility-based sizing) contained here?

2. Exit Logic
Likely implemented as:

Secondary loops inside TCL or alongside TEC

exit-condition.service.ts

order-manager.ts or trade-exit.service.ts

What to confirm:

Are exit conditions (take-profit, stop-loss, trailing stops) handled in TCL?

Are trade close events being generated in TCL?

3. Trade Execution Controller (TEC)
Likely implemented as:

execution-controller.ts

order-executor.ts or similar

What to confirm:

Does TEC handle partial fills, slippage, price-limit logic?

Does TEC currently take signals from TCL or does it do sizing?

4. Testing Artifacts
Look for tests such as:

tcl.spec.ts

execution-controller.spec.ts

position-sizing.spec.ts

Confirm whether existing tests assume TCL owns sizing/exits.

🔧 Separation Plan (Tasks)
Task 1 — Define Clear Responsibility Boundaries
TCL (Trade Control Loop) — only:

Monitor readyToBuy pool.

Promote signals that passed SQE into executions by sending them to TEC.

Update signal status to in flight or queued for execution.

TEC (Trade Execution Controller) — exclusively:

Determine position size.

Place orders (entry orders, partial fills).

Manage stop-loss, take-profit, trailing stop logic.

Handle fills, confirmations, cancellations.

Monitor open trades and send real-time status back to UI/telemetry.

Task 2 — Move Adaptive/Position Sizing into TEC
Steps:

Extract sizing logic

Update TCL to call TEC
Instead of:

executeOrder(signal, size);
Replace with:

Add Adapter/Wire
In TEC, for example:

async executeSignal(signal) {
  const size = await this.determinePositionSize(signal);
  return this.placeEntryOrder(signal, size);
}
Deprecate extra sizing methods
Remove deprecated sizing utilities from TCL context.

Task 3 — Move Exit Logic into TEC
Identify exit triggers that are currently TCL responsibilities:

Stop-loss

Time-based exits

function getExitCondition(trade) { ... }
function monitorOpenTrades() {

}
Ensure TEC handles:

Task 4 — Update Communication Patterns
TCL → TEC

TCL publishes signals to TEC via an event or API call:

EXECUTION_STARTED

Task 5 — Testing & Validation

Dawn Trader Architect (Chaplet Grounded) said:
This is an excellent and important clarification — and your assessment of the current drift is 100% correct.

Let’s ground this back to your canonical architecture and locked roadmap, using the repository structure and bridge documentation. I’ve re-grounded using the canonical Phase 11 definitions (TCL = Trade Criteria Limiter, TEC = Trade Execution Controller), and I’ll clarify each of the following:

✅ What exposure, correlation, and cooldown checks actually mean — and where they should happen.

✅ What the TCO (Trade Control Operator) really is and whether it’s a valid component.

✅ Clarify how adaptive sizing works and how it differs from signal sizing.

✅ Clarify what the FIFO queue is doing and whether it belongs in TEC (it doesn’t, per your design).

✅ Clarify the shared interfaces Replit mentioned and what they’re actually sharing.

✅ Correct Directive 11.0 implementation alignment to your roadmap.

✅ Provide specific correction actions for Replit (and the codebase) so that the structure goes back to being consistent with your architectural intent.

🧭 1. What “Exposure, Correlation, and Cooldowns” Mean — and Why They Shouldn’t Be in TCL
These checks are SQE-level gating mechanisms that exist before a signal enters the Ready-to-Buy (RTB) queue.

✔ Exposure
This ensures the engine isn’t taking too many trades that collectively exceed the global risk or slot limit.
Example:

If there are 8 open trade slots and all are filled, the exposure limit is reached, and no new trades can be opened.

This should not be recalculated inside TCL. It’s monitored by the SQE and surfaced through the RTB queue (signals already qualified are guaranteed exposure-compliant).

✔ Correlation
Correlation filters prevent multiple signals that are highly correlated (e.g., BTC/USD and ETH/USD) from being promoted together.

Again, this is handled at the SQE or pre-signal institutional math layer, not at the TCL level.
Once a signal reaches RTB, it’s already passed correlation gating.

✔ Cooldowns
Cooldown checks prevent immediate re-entry on the same asset shortly after an exit.
The SQE logs a “cooldown” flag as part of its rejection reason.

Once a signal reappears in RTB, it’s past its cooldown period and eligible for promotion.

✅ Therefore, none of these checks belong in TCL — TCL is not a filter.
It’s an event-driven promotion system based on slot availability and rank ordering, just as you described.

🧩 2. What Is the “TCO” (Trade Control Operator)?
Short answer: it’s unnecessary.

The “TCO” that Replit mentioned seems to have been created as an intermediate “pass-through” class between the TCL and the TEC.
However, your canonical architecture (and the bridge documentation) defines only two control layers:

TCL (Trade Criteria Limiter) — controls when and which signals are promoted from RTB into open trades, based on event triggers.

TEC (Trade Execution Controller) — handles trade lifecycle once a trade is open (execution, monitoring, trailing exits, etc.).

The addition of a TCO adds a redundant handoff layer that doesn’t exist in your design and could increase latency or confusion.
All promotion logic already belongs in the TCL. The TEC only engages once the signal is officially promoted.

✅ Recommendation: Remove the trade-control-operator.ts file and merge its logic (if any) back into criteria-limiter.ts.

⚙️ 3. How Adaptive Sizing Works — and Why It’s TEC-Scoped
Let’s clarify this distinction because it’s one of the most misunderstood pieces.

Static / Predictive Sizing (Phase 11.3 — Sizing Engine)
Happens before the signal ever reaches RTB.

Per your roadmap, it’s done in /server/services/sizing-engine.ts.

Works alongside the Signal Orchestrator and SQE.

Computes the initial signal.positionSize based on risk, confidence, volatility, and friction.

Example:

A signal has Confidence = 0.9, RegimeWeight = 0.8, BaseRisk = 1%.
Predictive sizing formula:
Risk = BaseRisk × PredictiveConfidence × RegimeWeight
⇒ Risk = 1% × 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.72% of account equity.
That becomes the signal’s positionSize and is stored in its signal object.

This sizing happens once and is part of the signal creation pipeline.

Adaptive Sizing (TEC Responsibility)
Adaptive sizing happens after a trade is already open.
It adjusts active trade exposure dynamically based on performance, trailing exits, and conditions.

Example:

A position is up +3%.
The TEC applies adaptive scaling:

Increase size slightly (+10%) if confidence improves and volatility stabilizes.

Or reduce exposure (−20%) if market volatility spikes.

This is reactive, not predictive, and is purely execution control logic — the TEC monitors this continuously and applies changes as conditions evolve.

✅ So yes — the TEC should only manage adaptive sizing after trade entry, not initial position sizing.
That aligns with your roadmap: 11.3 (Predictive Sizing) will handle the signal-based sizing engine.

🚫 4. FIFO Queue — Why It Doesn’t Belong
The “FIFO queue” Replit added to TEC is another artifact that doesn’t align with your system logic.

FIFO (First-In-First-Out) queues are used for job processing systems where tasks must be handled sequentially in time order.
That model doesn’t fit trading, where:

Open trades run concurrently.

Exits are based on market conditions, not order of entry.

Trades close independently.

✅ Recommendation: Remove the FIFO queue in TEC.
Each trade object should simply enter a Trade Registry and be managed individually until exit conditions are met.
No queuing or prioritization is required.

🧩 5. Shared Interfaces — Clarified
Replit mentioned “Shared Interfaces” in server/core/interfaces/trade-flow.ts.
That likely refers to shared data contracts between services — for example:

interface TradeSignal {
  id: string;
  symbol: string;
  confidence: number;
  regimeWeight: number;
  finalScore: number;
  positionSize: number;
}

interface TradeIntent {
  signalId: string;
  entryPrice: number;
  timestamp: string;
}

interface ActiveTrade {
  intentId: string;
  size: number;
  stopLoss: number;
  takeProfit: number;
}
These are not “shared interfaces” in the architectural sense — they are TypeScript data contracts shared across components (SQE, TCL, TEC).
They simply enforce consistent typing between modules (not shared runtime functionality).

✅ Recommendation: Rename that directory to server/types/trade-flow.ts to avoid confusion with architectural “interfaces”.

🧩 6. Corrected Directive 11.0 Scope
Here’s the corrected scope that keeps everything aligned with your roadmap:

⚙️ Directive 11.0 — Trade Criteria Limiter & Execution Controller Separation
Objective
Separate promotion logic (TCL) from execution and exit logic (TEC) while keeping signal-based sizing in the orchestration pipeline.

Implementation Rules
✅ TCL:

Monitors open trade slots (max concurrent trades).

Triggers on two events:

Two-minute failsafe interval.

Fifteen signals accumulated in the Ready-to-Buy queue.

Promotes the highest-ranked signals into open slots.

Performs no filtering — SQE has already validated all conditions.

✅ TEC:

Manages open trades after entry.

Handles adaptive trailing exits and stop-loss enforcement.

Tracks trade lifecycle and communicates closures to telemetry.

🚫 Remove:

TCO layer (redundant).

FIFO queuing (not relevant to parallel trade lifecycle).

Sizing logic (handled in Phase 11.3).

TCO layer	Exists in /core/operators/	Delete. TCL handles promotion directly.
FIFO Queue	Implemented in TEC	Remove; manage trades individually.
Sizing in TEC	Present	Restrict to trailing exit adjustments only.
Shared Interfaces	Ambiguous	Rename to /types/trade-flow.ts (data contracts).

⚙️ Directive 11.0C — SQE & TEC Stabilization and Schema Normalization

Signal Type III – Pure Pattern
Purpose: Structural recognition of chart geometry without quantitative confirmation.
Objective: Detect visually derived formations validated by historical pattern success rates.

🧠 Regime Mapping
Market Regime	Metrics	Active Strategies	Mathematical Framework
Bullish Pattern Regime	Price above SMA 50, Pattern = Bull Flag or Triangle	Bull Flag (BF), Ascending Triangle (AT)	Angle of slope > 20°, PatternScore ≥ 0.7
Bearish Pattern Regime	Price below SMA 50, Pattern = Bear Flag or Descending Triangle	Bear Flag (BE), Descending Triangle (DT)	Angle < −20°, PatternScore ≥ 0.7
Compression Pattern (Neutral)	ATR contraction > 25 %, Pattern = Symmetrical Triangle	Symmetrical Triangle (ST)	σ compression → break probability calc.
🧩 How the Strategy System Works
1️⃣ Filtered Pairs → Signal Candidates
FX5 output passes Institutional Guards (LQ, VolNoise, ρ).

2️⃣ Signal Orchestrator Builds Features
Each pair → signal object with Confidence, HybridScore, RegimeWeight, PatternScore.

3️⃣ SQE Filters
Threshold gates: FinalScore ≥ θ_f, RegimeWeight ≥ θ_r.

4️⃣ RTB Queue Ranking
Sorted by FinalScore; each entry tagged with signal type & strategy.

5️⃣ TCL Promotion
Event triggered on open-slot availability; selects top ranked signal overall.

6️⃣ TEC Execution
Applies adaptive positioning and trailing logic.

7️⃣ Telemetry Learning
Records outcomes → updates confidence weights per signal type and strategy.

💰 17️⃣ Position Sizing System (Predictive Risk Engine)
🎯 Purpose
Position sizing determines how much capital to allocate per trade while maintaining consistent portfolio risk.
The system balances statistical expectancy, volatility normalization, and predictive confidence to dynamically scale exposure.

A. Where Sizing Is Calculated
1️⃣ Primary Calculation:

Performed inside the Signal Orchestrator, before signals enter the SQE.

The result is stored in each signal as signal.positionSize and signal.riskExposure.

2️⃣ Adaptive Adjustments:

Applied later by the Trade Execution Controller (TEC) during live trade management.

Adjustments are trend-based only (±10 %), using trendline reinforcement/weakness feedback.

3️⃣ Predictive Input Source:

Predictive confidence and volatility data originate from the Telemetry Learning Engine, which updates adaptive weights after every closed trade.

🔟 Signal Types, Regimes & Strategies
Signal Type I – Quantitative
Driven by numeric models and momentum analysis.

Regime	Metrics	Strategies
Bullish	EMA20>EMA50, ADX>25	Breakout (BR), VWAP Continuation (VWAP-C)
Bearish	EMA20<EMA50, ADX>25	Short Breakout (SBR), Pullback Re-entry
Range	ADX<20, Low ATR	Mean Reversion (MR), VWAP Bounce
Volatile	ATR↑10%, Vol↑30%	Volatility Breakout (VBO)
Signal Type II – Hybrid (Quant × Pattern)

🧩 Part 1 – FX5 Scanner & Adaptive Filtering
🧠 1.1 Purpose and Functional Overview
The FX5 Scanner is the entry point of DawnTrader’s trading intelligence pipeline.
Its role is to continuously analyze the available trading universe, compute standardized market features, and identify pairs exhibiting measurable trade potential.

It does not decide what strategy to use or whether to trade — it simply ensures that only viable, data-rich pairs proceed to the next layer (the Institutional Guards and Decision Strategy Selector (DSS)).

🎯 Core Objectives
Continuously monitor all candidate pairs.

Quantify key structural attributes — price movement, liquidity, volatility, and stability.

Identify market regime context (Bullish, Bearish, Neutral).

Adapt scanning intensity and pair inclusion dynamically based on system performance and global regime alignment.

⚙️ 1.2 System Role in the Architecture
The FX5 Scanner sits at the very top of the DawnTrader signal generation chain:

Market Feeds → FX5 Scanner → Institutional Guards → DSS (Signal Orchestrator) → SQE → RTB → TCL → TEC → Telemetry
Each stage downstream depends on the completeness and normalization of FX5’s feature output.
FX5 is therefore both a filter and a feature generator.

🧩 1.3 Data Inputs
Input Source	Data Type	Description
Market Data Feeds	OHLCV	Raw price, volume, and spread data for each pair
Exchange Metadata	Market depth, tick size, quote currency	Used for liquidity and slippage modeling
Historical Snapshot Cache	Rolling 24-hour candle history	Used for volatility and ATR calculations
Telemetry Feedback	Adaptive weights	Used for adaptive scanning prioritization

🧠 Part 2 – Decision Strategy Selector (DSS) & Signal Orchestration
2.1 Purpose & Role in the System Flow
The DSS (Signal Orchestrator) is the decision-making brain of DawnTrader’s predictive pipeline.

It receives the Filtered Pool of qualified trading pairs from Part 1 and:

Determines each pair’s dominant market regime (Bullish, Bearish, Neutral, Volatile).

Assigns a Signal Type (Quantitative, Hybrid, Pattern-based).

Selects the optimal strategy for that signal type + regime combination.

Calculates the strategic features that quantify trade quality (HybridScore, Confidence, RegimeWeight, Decay).

Packages the data into a standardized Signal Object for SQE evaluation.

Input → Output Context
[Filtered Pool]
    ↓
[DSS / Signal Orchestrator]
    ↓
[SQE → RTB → TCL → TEC]

2.3 Signal Types and Their Objectives
Signal Type	Primary Focus	Objective	Key Inputs
Quantitative (Q)	Momentum & statistical edges	Exploit price-momentum and liquidity imbalances	EMA crossovers, ADX, ATR, volume delta
Hybrid (H)	Quant + Pattern fusion	Combine numerical signals with pattern recognition confirmation	Quant scores + pattern probabilities
Pattern (P)	Structural geometry	Identify chart formations implying reversals or breakouts	Price shape vectors, slope ratios, RSI dynamics
2.4 Market Regimes by Signal Type & Associated Strategies
(1) Quantitative Signals (Q)
Market Regime	Defining Metrics	Active Strategies	Mathematical Notes
Bullish Trend	EMA20 > EMA50, ADX > 25	Breakout (BR), VWAP Continuation (VWAP-C)	Momentum ≈ (EMA20−EMA50)/EMA50; Signal if > 0.015
Bearish Trend	EMA20 < EMA50, ADX > 25	Short Breakout (SBR), Pullback Re-entry	Same logic mirrored for shorts
Range	ADX < 20, ATR flat	Mean Reversion (MR), VWAP Bounce	RegimeWeight ∝ 1 −
Volatile	ATR↑ > 10 %, Vol↑ > 30 %	Volatility Breakout (VBO)	Edge ∝ ATR / Spread %
(2) Hybrid Signals (H)
Market Regime	Defining Metrics	Active Strategies	Description
Bullish Consolidation	RSI 40–60, EMA alignment	Breakout Pattern (BR-P), Channel Continuation	Pattern prob > 0.7 and Quant Momentum > 0
Bearish Reversal	RSI > 70 → cross < 60	Mean Reversion Pattern (MR-P), H&S	Pattern shift triggers HybridScore drop
Transitional Regime	Vol ↓ 15 %, ADX flat	Regime Shift, VWAP Transition	Neutral phase used for re-balancing signals
(3) Pattern Signals (P)
Market Regime	Metrics	Strategies	Notes
Bullish Pattern	Price > SMA50	Bull Flag, Ascending Triangle	Probability = area overlap × slope consistency
Bearish Pattern	Price < SMA50	Bear Flag, Descending Triangle	Reversal signal if volume > avg×1.2
Neutral/Compression	ATR contract > 25 %	Symmetrical Triangle	Potential break both ways → Dual Signal Tag

🧩 1.9 Conclusion & Summary
The FX5 Scanner and Adaptive Filtering Layer establishes the foundation of DawnTrader’s entire intelligence pipeline.
It transforms raw market data into a quantitatively validated universe of trade-ready pairs and continuously tunes its own sensitivity according to real-time regime feedback.

🔑 Core Principles
Quality over Quantity — FX5 doesn’t scan every market equally; it targets pairs with measurable opportunity density.

Institutional Rigor — Every asset must satisfy Liquidity, Noise, and Correlation guards before any trading logic engages.

Adaptive Focus — Scan allocation shifts dynamically based on global regime alignment and recent success ratios.

Regime Awareness — The scanner interprets market states (Bullish, Bearish, Neutral) and directs computational focus accordingly.

Telemetry Integration — Continuous feedback loops inform the adaptive weights, ensuring FX5 “learns” from trading outcomes.

📦 Deliverables to Downstream Layers
Output	Description
Filtered Pool	List of pairs that pass Institutional Guards
Feature Vectors	Normalized metrics (momentum, volume, volatility, etc.) for each pair
Global Regime Metric	Weighted average of pair-level regime scores for adaptive balancing
Scan Weights	Dynamic prioritization values for the DSS
Telemetry Stream	Feedback data to update adaptive coefficients and regime models
Together, these outputs form the input foundation for the DSS / Signal Orchestrator, which decides what kind of trade to initiate, why, and how strongly the system should believe in it.
