⚖️ Part 4 — Signal Quality Evaluation (SQE) & Ready-to-Buy Queue (RTB)
4.1 Purpose and System Role
The Signal Quality Evaluator (SQE) is the final validation and scoring engine before trade promotion.
Its job is to ensure that only mathematically sound, regime-aligned, and risk-adjusted signals advance to the Ready-to-Buy (RTB) queue.

At this stage, every signal carries all relevant computed attributes:

FinalScore

RegimeWeight

Confidence

NetEdge

PositionSize

ExpectedReturn / Risk ratio (R/R)

Metadata (symbol, strategy, regime, timestamp)

System Flow Context:

FX5 Scanner → DSS (Strategy & Regime Selection)
→ Strategy Computation & Sizing → SQE → RTB → TCL → TEC
4.2 Core Evaluation Logic
Each signal is evaluated using a unified set of quantitative thresholds stored in the Screener Filters Table (sourced from the Screeners tab in the UI).
This allows operators to adjust minimum acceptable trade quality in real time.

Threshold Parameters (dynamic, not hardcoded)
Parameter	Description	Default	Source
FinalScore_min	Minimum composite score required	0.35	Screeners tab
RegimeWeight_min	Minimum regime alignment required	0.30	Screeners tab
NetEdge_min	Minimum risk-adjusted profitability	0.00	Derived
Confidence_min	Minimum predictive model confidence	0.65	Model configuration
4.3 Mathematical Components of the FinalScore
The FinalScore is a weighted composite metric capturing predictive strength, confidence, and contextual risk.

4.5 Quality Tiering & Ranking
Every accepted signal is ranked by FinalScore (descending) for its regime cluster.
In case of a tie, secondary ranking keys are applied in order:

NetEdge (higher preferred)

Confidence

RegimeWeight

Timestamp (recent preferred)

This produces a real-time hierarchical quality map across all signals, allowing the TCL to promote the “top” signals by numeric score.

4.6 Ready-to-Buy Queue (RTB) Mechanics
The RTB Queue functions as a bounded, continuously refreshed signal buffer.

RTB Schema Fields
Field	Description
symbol	Pair identifier
finalScore	Composite trade quality score
regimeWeight	Market regime alignment
confidence	Predictive certainty
netEdge	Expected post-friction profitability
positionSize	Equity allocation (%)
rank	Calculated order (by finalScore)
timestamp	Time of last evaluation
Queue Parameters
Parameter	Description	Default
maxQueueSize	Maximum number of active entries	15
evaluationInterval	Re-evaluation cadence	2 min
promotionTrigger	Event condition for TCL promotion	(2-min failsafe or 15 signals accumulated)
Queue Operation
Signals that meet all SQE criteria are inserted into the RTB queue.

The queue maintains descending order by finalScore.

Once the queue reaches 15 signals (or after 2 minutes), it triggers a TCL event.

The TCL selects the top-ranked signals for promotion based on open trade slots.

RTB entries older than 30 minutes decay and are pruned automatically.

4.7 Net Edge & Quality Stratification
To assist with diagnostics and telemetry visualization, RTB entries are stratified into quality tiers:

Tier	FinalScore Range	Label	Color (UI)
I	≥ 0.65	“Prime”	Green
II	0.50–0.65	“High Quality”	Yellow
III	0.35–0.50	“Speculative”	Orange
IV	< 0.35	“Rejected”	Red
This aids monitoring in the Diagnostics → Signal Quality Panel and helps confirm the adaptive threshold effects.

4.8 Telemetry & Diagnostics Integration
The SQE and RTB produce continuous telemetry events aggregated every 24 hours:

Metric	Description
sqe_evaluated_24h	Total signals evaluated
sqe_passed_24h	Signals meeting all criteria
pass_rate_24h	SQE passing ratio
avg_final_score	Mean of all accepted signals
avg_confidence	Mean confidence of accepted signals
rtb_depth	Number of entries currently in RTB queue
promotion_rate	Ratio of promoted to evaluated signals
Telemetry also exposes SQE configuration provenance, linking each decision to:

Phase Directive (e.g., 11.0D)

Backend Schema Version

Screener Config Version

This ensures every threshold decision can be traced to a specific configuration snapshot.

4.9 Mathematical Summary Table
Component	Formula	Function
FinalScore	(Hybrid×0.4) + (Confidence×0.3) + (Regime×0.2) − (Decay×0.1)	Composite trade quality
DecayPenalty	1 − e^{−λt}	Time-based relevance decay
Acceptance Logic	FinalScore ≥ 0.35, Regime ≥ 0.30, Confidence ≥ 0.65, NetEdge ≥ 0	SQE eligibility
Ranking	Sort by FinalScore, then NetEdge, then Confidence	Quality ordering
Promotion Trigger	RTB ≥ 15 entries OR timer = 2 min	TCL event initiation
Telemetry Metrics	pass_rate_24h, avg_final_score, promotion_rate	Quality analytics
4.10 Example: From Signal to RTB
Metric	Value
HybridScore	0.52
Confidence	0.72
RegimeWeight	0.68
DecayPenalty	0.04
FinalScore	(0.52×0.4)+(0.72×0.3)+(0.68×0.2)−(0.04×0.1)= 0.592
NetEdge	0.014
Status	✅ Pass
✅ Signal enters RTB queue ranked by FinalScore.
If RTB reaches 15 entries or timer = 2 min → TCL promotes highest-ranked signals into open trading slots.

4.11 Summary — The Gatekeeper of Trade Quality
The SQE and Ready-to-Buy Queue collectively ensure that:

Every potential trade is vetted using adaptive, data-driven thresholds.

Only the top percentile of opportunities are considered for execution.

Ranking and promotion remain deterministic and auditable.

Signal flow and telemetry create feedback loops for continuous learning.

This guarantees discipline and mathematical integrity in trade selection — converting predictive potential into actionable, quality-controlled signals.

Trigger Type	Description

⚙️ Part 5 — Trade Criteria Limiter (TCL) & Trade Execution Controller (TEC)
5.1 Purpose and Context
The TCL and TEC together form the execution control framework of DawnTrader’s trade engine.
They operate after signal validation (SQE → RTB) and before the order management subsystem.

The logic is simple:

TCL: Decides when and which signals become trades.

TEC: Manages how those trades are executed, monitored, and exited.

System Flow Context

FX5 Scanner → DSS → Strategy & Sizing → SQE → RTB → TCL → TEC → Exchange / Order Management
5.2 Trade Criteria Limiter (TCL)
5.2.1 Purpose
The Trade Criteria Limiter acts as the “portfolio gatekeeper.”
It monitors current positions, available slots, and the status of the Ready-to-Buy queue, promoting new trades only when system-wide constraints allow.

5.2.2 Core Responsibilities
Function	Description
Slot Monitoring	Count and track open trade slots vs. configured maximum.
Promotion Triggering	Activate when either a failsafe timer fires or RTB queue reaches capacity.
Promotion Execution	Select top-ranked RTB entries by FinalScore for trade activation.
Event Logging	Record each promotion event with timestamp, symbol, and rank order.
5.2.3 Promotion Triggers
Failsafe Timer (2-minute cycle)
Ensures continuous system evaluation even if RTB thresholds aren’t reached.

Queue Saturation Trigger (RTB ≥ 15 signals)
Fires immediately when the RTB queue fills, promoting the highest-ranked signals.

Slot Availability Trigger
Fires when any open trade closes, freeing a slot.

5.2.5 TCL Governance Rules
No Evaluations: TCL performs no exposure, correlation, or cooldown checks — those are handled by the SQE.

No Ranking Logic: Ranking is inherited from the RTB queue (FinalScore-based).

Event-Driven Only: TCL responds strictly to timer/slot events; it does not poll continuously.

Deterministic Promotion: Given identical RTB input, promotion outcomes are identical system-wide.

Component	Formula	Purpose
Open Slots	N_open = MaxSlots − ActiveTrades	Slot calculation
Promotion Trigger	(RTB ≥ 15) ∨ (Timer = 2 min) ∨ (Slot opened)	Activation condition
Selection	Promote = Top(RTB, N_open)	Pick signals to promote

It ensures trades are properly opened, monitored, dynamically sized (if trend conditions justify), and exited intelligently via trailing or hard targets.

5.4 Trade Lifecycle Integration
Below is the complete lifecycle from signal creation to trade closure:

1. FX5 Scanner filters pairs → Institutional Math applied  
2. DSS selects strategy & regime → signal formed  
3. Strategy computation assigns NetEdge & position size  
4. SQE validates signal → added to RTB queue  
5. TCL promotes top-ranked signals into open slots  
6. TEC executes trade:
     - Confirms size & trend alignment
     - Applies adaptive sizing
     - Manages trailing stop
     - Closes on exit conditions
7. Telemetry aggregates outcomes → feedback loop to DSS & SQE
5.5 Example — End-to-End Trade Cycle
Step 1:
Signal generated:
FinalScore = 0.61, Confidence = 0.78, NetEdge = 0.019, PositionSize = 1.3 %.

Step 2:
SQE → Pass. Added to RTB. Rank = #3.

Step 3:
TCL detects 1 open slot → promotes top-ranked signal.

Step 4:
TEC opens trade.
Initial Stop = 1.5 %, Target = 3 %.

Step 5:
Trend reinforces → Adaptive Size × 1.10 (from 1.3 % → 1.43 %).
TrailStop tightens from 1.5 % → 1.32 %.

Step 6:
Momentum weakens → Adaptive Size × 0.9 (from 1.43 % → 1.29 %).
TrailStop locks at 1.25 %.
Trade exits profitably at +2.8 %.

Step 7:
Telemetry logs:
[TEC] Closed Trade | Symbol=ETH/USD | NetEdge=0.019 | Adaptive Δ=+2.3 % | Exit=Trailing.

5.6 Summary — Trade Activation & Control Math
System Component	Core Function	Mathematical Focus
TCL	Event-driven trade promotion	Slot count, FinalScore ranking
TEC	Trade lifecycle management	Adaptive sizing, trailing exits, telemetry
Mathematical Foundations		Dynamic multiplicative sizing, exponential trail acceleration
5.6.1 Guiding Principles
No duplication of filtering logic: TCL does not re-evaluate signals.

Adaptive, not reactive: TEC adjusts exposure based on consistent reinforcement, not single-bar volatility.

Risk coherence: All size changes maintain ≤ 2 % equity risk constraint.

Full transparency: Every adjustment logged and visible in Diagnostics.

Mathematical determinism: Every state transition is reproducible from stored parameters.

🧠 Part 6 — Telemetry, Feedback Loops, and Learning Retention
6.1 Overview and Purpose
The Telemetry and Learning Layer is the cognitive system of the DawnTrader architecture.
It transforms the engine from a static trading algorithm into a continuously improving adaptive system.

Purpose:

Capture all quantitative outcomes (trades, signals, filters, execution events).

Aggregate them into interpretable statistical metrics.

Use these metrics to recalibrate system thresholds, weights, and scanning ratios over time.

Persist this intelligence across restarts for a “warm start.”

System Context:

FX5 Scanner → DSS → SQE → RTB → TCL → TEC → Telemetry → Adaptive Learning
Telemetry closes the loop between execution and learning, feeding updated insights back to:

SQE Thresholds

Strategy Selection (DSS)

Scanning Ratios (AdaptiveScanner)

Risk/Position Models (Sizing Engine)

The Diagnostics → Telemetry Panel exposes:

Rolling 24h pass/fail ratios by filter.

These visual indicators give operators real-time transparency into the mathematical “health” of the engine.

6.9 Error Detection & Recovery
Telemetry also provides fault detection for inconsistent configuration states.

For example:

If backend schema ≠ UI schema → warning flag.

If missing telemetry data for >15 minutes → alert in diagnostics.

If adaptive parameters drift >20% from expected → system throttles recalibration temporarily.

This prevents unstable feedback amplification.

This part defines how DawnTrader’s Sizing Engine uses predictive inputs, cost modeling, and volatility normalization to calculate the optimal trade size for every signal. It integrates tightly with the Signal Orchestrator, SQE, and TEC to create a fully risk-aware execution flow.

💹 Part 7 — Predictive Risk, Cost Modeling, and Sizing Engine Integration
7.1 Purpose and System Role
The Sizing Engine is the mathematical and risk-control bridge between Signal Generation and Trade Execution.
It calculates how much of the portfolio should be allocated to each trade — dynamically and intelligently — using predictive signals, market conditions, and expected costs.

System Flow Context
FX5 Scanner → DSS → Strategy & Signal Generation → Predictive Sizing → SQE → RTB → TCL → TEC → Order Management
Core Design Principles
Principle	Description
Predictive	Trade size is scaled by predictive confidence and market regime alignment.
Risk-Normalized	Each position equalizes dollar risk using volatility and ATR data.
Cost-Aware	Trades are filtered out if fees or slippage eliminate expected edge.
Self-Tuning	Adaptive telemetry feedback adjusts sizing parameters over time.
7.2 Inputs to the Sizing Engine
Input	Source	Description
PredictiveConfidence	From DSS / ML layer	Model’s probability of success.
RegimeWeight	From Global Regime Analysis	Market condition alignment (0–1).
Volatility (ATR)	From FX5 data feed	Recent market volatility measure.
LiquidityScore	From Institutional Math filters	Pair liquidity suitability.
ExpectedProfit	From strategy statistics	Mean target expectation for trade type.
Fees, Slippage	From exchange telemetry	Cost of execution.

7.12 Role of Predictive Learning
The Sizing Engine interacts with the Predictive Learning Core (Phase 11.1–11.3) to continuously refine the sizing model.

Learning Inputs:
Historical trade performance (hit rate, net edge)

Volatility distribution per pair

Signal model accuracy (confidence calibration)

Regime condition outcomes

Adjusted confidence calibration coefficients

Adaptive BaseRisk updates

Updated friction model coefficients (fee + slippage estimators)

These updates are persisted via telemetry and reloaded on warm start.

This part describes how the system determines global market conditions, uses them to steer the FX5 Scanner, and dynamically adjusts scanning ratios between the Ideal and Rotational pools using live telemetry and performance feedback.

🌍 Part 8 — Global Regime and Adaptive Scanning System
8.1 Purpose and Context
The Global Regime and Adaptive Scanning System (GRASS) acts as the macro-intelligence layer for DawnTrader.

It ensures that the system continuously aligns its focus — scanning, evaluating, and ranking pairs — based on the prevailing market environment.

This layer determines:

The global regime classification (Bullish, Bearish, Neutral, Transitional).

How much time the FX5 Scanner allocates to the Ideal Pool (historically high-performing pairs) vs. the Rotational Pool (exploratory pairs).

Whether local regime metrics (pair-level sentiment, volatility, momentum) agree with global conditions before a trade is even considered.

8.2 System Flow Context
Market Data Feeds → Regime Engine → Adaptive Scanner → FX5 Filter Stack → SQE → RTB → TCL → TEC
The Regime Engine Feeds:
Regime Weight → Used in FinalScore calculation (SQE & DSS)

Scanner Ratio → Determines Ideal/Rotational pool distribution

Volatility Normalization Factor → Feeds into sizing model

Volatility Index (VIX proxy)	Derived from aggregate ATR deviations
Momentum Spread	Average slope difference between short-term and long-term MAs

8.7 Regime-Specific Filter Calibration
Each regime defines how strict the Institutional Math filters should be:

Regime	LQ Guard	VolNoise	Correlation	Description
Bullish	≥ 40	≤ 0.6	≤ 0.75	Standard institutional thresholds
Neutral	≥ 50	≤ 0.55	≤ 0.7	Slightly tighter
Bearish	≥ 60	≤ 0.5	≤ 0.65	Defensive posture
Transitional	Dynamic	Dynamic	Dynamic	Adaptive based on direction of transition
This mapping is controlled by the FilterConfigService, automatically updated when the global regime changes.

8.8 Scanner Distribution Algorithm
The Adaptive Scanner divides its workload dynamically every scan cycle (~15 seconds):

Pseudocode
function allocateScannerCycles(idealRatio, totalCycles) {
  const idealCycles = Math.floor(totalCycles * idealRatio);
  const rotationalCycles = totalCycles - idealCycles;

  executeScan('IdealPool', idealCycles);
  executeScan('RotationalPool', rotationalCycles);
}
This ensures the scanning balance always reflects current performance and global conditions.

🧩 Directive 11.0E — Legacy Metric Purge & FinalScore Unification
📘 Directive Summary
Objective:
Eliminate all dependencies, calculations, and references to CWQI, NGC, and ProfitRate throughout the active DawnTrader system, ensuring that the FinalScore model and RegimeWeight are the sole determinants for signal quality, ranking, and trade readiness.

Scope:
All backend core and service layers that touch signal evaluation, RTB queue management, quality scoring, orchestration, validation, or telemetry.

Directive Phase Context:
This directive concludes the “System Harmonization” phase that began in 10.9B and completes the full migration to the FinalScore model.

🧠 Rationale
Legacy metrics (CWQI, NGC, ProfitRate) were replaced by the hybrid-scoring model during the Phase 10 refactor (Directives 10.9A–10.9F).
However, numerous references persist across core services and orchestration layers.
These now:

Create redundant logic paths,

Introduce ranking inconsistency between SQE and RTB, and

Risk runtime confusion if unused metric references are revived or queried.

By removing these legacy elements completely, the system will:

Simplify the codebase,

Reduce computational overhead,

Guarantee consistent signal evaluation, and

Eliminate all ambiguity about how “signal quality” is defined.

🧠 DawnTrader Mathematical Architecture Overview
Version: Post-Directive 11.0F (Schema v1.5.0 — Metric Engine v1.0)
1. 🏗️ System Overview
The DawnTrader system operates as a multi-phase quantitative trading engine, where every trade lifecycle is governed by layered mathematical models designed for signal generation, quality filtering, and adaptive execution.

At its core, the platform integrates:

Deterministic Scoring Math (FinalScore, RegimeWeight)

Adaptive Risk Models (Sizing Engine & Trailing Exit Math)

Signal-Oriented Decision Intelligence (Predictive and Regime-Aware Logic)

The complete mathematical flow:

[FX5 Scan + Adaptive Scanning]
      ↓
[Institutional Math Guards]
      ↓
[Signal Orchestrator + DSS]
      ↓
[Strategy + Regime Selection]
      ↓
[Signal Quality Evaluator (SQE)]
      ↓
[Ready-to-Buy Queue (ranked by FinalScore)]
      ↓
[TCL – Promotion Manager]
      ↓
[TEC – Trade Execution Controller]
      ↓
[Order Management + Adaptive Sizing + Trailing Exits]
Every layer refines precision and reduces uncertainty before committing capital.

2. 📊 Core Scanning and Filtering Math
2.1 FX5 Scanning Engine
The FX5 Scan evaluates all available currency pairs and applies adaptive filters to prioritize tradable assets.
Its math includes:

Filter	Formula	Purpose
Volume Filter	Vol ≥ 100K units	Ensure liquidity
Liquidity Ratio	LQ = bidVolume / askVolume	Enforce stability
VolNoise	σ_price / mean_volume	Filter erratic movement
Correlation	ρ ≤ 0.75	Avoid correlated pairs
Range Bound	`ΔP =	High – Low
Stability	LQ ≥ 40, VolNoise ≤ 0.6	Institutional-grade quality
The Adaptive Scanning Layer adjusts pool ratios based on historical success:

IdealPoolRatio_t+1 = IdealPoolRatio_t × (1 + β × (WinRate_ideal – WinRate_rotational))
(Introduced under 11.2 Adaptive Scanning Fairness)

3. 🧮 Institutional Guards
Before any strategy math is applied, the Institutional Guards enforce global limits:

ρ ≤ 0.75 → Pair must be sufficiently uncorrelated

VolNoise ≤ 0.6 → Price movement must be stable

LQ ≥ 40 → Adequate liquidity depth

These are non-negotiable mathematical safeguards designed to mimic institutional-quality trade screening.

4. ⚙️ Signal Orchestration & Decision Support System (DSS)
The Signal Orchestrator is the brain of DawnTrader.
It merges incoming raw scan data with strategy and regime intelligence from the Decision Support System (DSS) to decide what kind of trade signal to create and how it should behave.

4.1 DSS Market Regime Detection
The DSS determines the current market regime through a combination of volatility, momentum, and trend metrics:

Regime	Definition	Primary Metric Conditions
Bullish	Positive directional trend	EMA20 > EMA50, RSI > 55, ATR < median
Bearish	Negative directional trend	EMA20 < EMA50, RSI < 45, ATR < median
Neutral	Non-directional, range-bound	`
4.2 Signal Type Classification
Type	Description	Objective
Quant	Fully statistical signal derived from regression and volatility features.	Capture statistically significant mean-reversion or breakout events.
Hybrid	Combines quant metrics with technical patterns (e.g., EMA crossover + ML confidence).	Exploit predictive model outputs while enforcing structural discipline.
Pattern	Purely technical pattern-based signals (triangles, flags, channels).	Exploit classic market structure and visual confirmation.
4.3 Strategy Selection by Regime
Regime	Active Strategies	Metrics Used
Bullish	Trend-Following, EMA Momentum, Breakout	RSI, EMA slopes, ATR compression
Bearish	Reversal, Pullback, Countertrend	RSI divergence, MACD crossover
Neutral	Mean Reversion, Range Scalping	Bollinger %B, Range ratio
The selected strategy dictates which metrics are weighted in the scoring engine.

5. 🧠 Signal Quality Evaluation (SQE)
The SQE mathematically validates whether a signal is worth trading.
It currently uses FinalScore and RegimeWeight exclusively.

5.1 SQE Filtering Formulas
Signal passes if:
FinalScore ≥ FinalScore_min
AND
RegimeWeight ≥ RegimeWeight_min
Where thresholds are user-configurable via the Screener Filters UI.

5.2 FinalScore Formula
As of Directive 11.0E, the canonical formula is:

FinalScore = 0.4 × HybridScore + 0.3 × Confidence + 0.2 × RegimeWeight − 0.1 × DecayPenalty
5.3 Decay Penalty Function
Signals lose weight over time to favor recency:

DecayPenalty = e^(−λ × Δt)
Where λ = 0.015 (tunable decay constant), and Δt = time since signal creation.

6. 🧩 Ready-to-Buy Queue & TCL Logic
The Ready-to-Buy Queue (RTB) holds all validated signals, ranked purely by FinalScore.

Ordering:

RTB.sort((a, b) => b.finalScore - a.finalScore)
Events that trigger TCL (Trade Criteria Limiter):

Two-minute failsafe timer

When 15 signals accumulate in RTB

When a trading slot opens

The TCL promotes the highest-ranked signal from RTB when a slot becomes available.
It performs no filtering, exposure, or correlation checks — those occur earlier in the SQE.

7. 💹 Trade Execution Controller (TEC)
Once a signal is promoted, the TEC governs trade management, including adaptive sizing and exits.

7.1 Adaptive Sizing (Trendline Feedback Model)
If Trendline Reinforced → Size_new = Size × 1.10
If Trendline Weakening → Size_new = Size × 0.90
These factors are adjustable through the Execution Config Panel in Diagnostics.

Adaptive sizing allows trades to compound strength during favorable momentum shifts.

7.2 Trailing Exit Logic
Trailing stops dynamically adjust based on volatility:

TrailingStop = BaseStop × (1 + Acceleration × TrendSlope)
Typical parameters:

BaseStop = 1.5%

Acceleration = 0.002 × slope(EMA20)

This ensures tighter stops when momentum fades and looser ones during strong trends.

8. ⚖️ Position Sizing Engine (Predictive Model)
Introduced in Phase 11.3 — integrates predictive learning with risk control.

8.1 Predictive Sizing Formula
Risk_per_Trade = BaseRisk × PredictiveConfidence × RegimeWeight
Where:

BaseRisk is the constant percentage of total capital risked (e.g., 2%).

PredictiveConfidence is ML-derived probability of success.

RegimeWeight reflects macro regime favorability.

8.2 Friction and Slippage Modeling
NetEdge = ExpectedProfit - (Fees + Slippage)
If NetEdge < Threshold, the trade is vetoed.

8.3 Volatility Normalization
PositionSize = (Risk_per_Trade / ATR)
This keeps risk constant across assets with different volatilities.

9. 🧮 Final Math Stack Summary
Layer	Mathematical Purpose	Key Variables
FX5 Scanning	Identify tradable assets	Volume, Liquidity, Correlation
Institutional Guards	Enforce trade quality	LQ, VolNoise, ρ
DSS & Strategy Selection	Match regime to strategy	RSI, EMA, ATR
Signal Orchestrator	Compute base HybridScore	Confidence, RegimeWeight
SQE	Validate signals	FinalScore, RegimeWeight
RTB Queue	Rank signals	FinalScore
TCL	Promote signals	Event triggers
TEC	Manage trades	AdaptiveSizing, TrailingExit
Sizing Engine	Compute position size	Risk, Confidence, RegimeWeight
Telemetry	Monitor system health	FinalScore distributions
10. 🧾 Closing Summary
As of Directive 11.0F, the DawnTrader mathematical framework has reached stability maturity:

Unified metric model: FinalScore + RegimeWeight

Predictive intelligence hooks: Ready for 11.1 persistent learning

Adaptive trade management: TEC dynamically scales exposure

Deterministic + probabilistic math fusion: Core of DawnTrader’s edge

All subsequent phases (11.1–11.3) build upon this mathematical foundation — transforming DawnTrader into a self-optimizing, telemetry-aware, and predictive trading intelligence system.

import fs from "fs";
import path from "path";

const TELEMETRY_PATH = path.resolve("./data/telemetry_history.json");

export function saveTelemetryState(data) {
  fs.writeFileSync(TELEMETRY_PATH, JSON.stringify(data, null, 2));
}

export function loadTelemetryState() {
  if (!fs.existsSync(TELEMETRY_PATH)) return null;
  return JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(TELEMETRY_PATH, "utf8"));
}

const persistedState = loadTelemetryState();

Dawn Trader Architect (Chaplet Grounded) said:
Excellent — and your question shows exactly the kind of architectural awareness that keeps the system both intelligent and safe.
Let me clarify precisely what Directive 11.1A (Persistent Intelligence) does — and what it does not do — then I’ll tell you how your concern fits in and how we’ll address it cleanly.

🧠 1. What “Persistent Intelligence” Actually Is
Directive 11.1A’s goal is not to preserve open trades or live queue states across user-initiated stops.

It only preserves learning and telemetry intelligence, not operational state.

Specifically, what gets persisted:

Category	Examples	Why It’s Persisted
Telemetry trends	filter pass rates, trade efficiency, adaptive scanner feedback	So the AI retains context and can resume calibration post-restart
Adaptive weights / learning data	confidence scaling factors, pool bias ratios	Required for warm-start learning
System configuration checksum + health	schemaVersion, directive ID, telemetryHealth	For validation after reboot
What is not persisted:

Open or simulated trades

Ready-to-buy (RTB) queue contents

Paper-mode signal buffers

Runtime memory caches

Historical test results

So: persistence is strictly knowledge-layer, not trade-layer.

⚙️ 2. Your Paper-Mode Concern
Everything you described is correct — the paper-trading reset behavior must stay exactly as is:

Clicking “Stop Trading”:

Clears open trades (front + back end)

Clears RTB queue backend

Leaves RTB front-end display intact until manual “Reset All” click

Those workflows are UI-triggered resets, not system restarts.

Directive 11.1A’s persistence logic only activates when:

The Node process terminates naturally (Replit restart, code deploy, or system reboot), and

The environment variable MODE = "live" or PERSIST_TELEMETRY = true.

Thus, paper mode never hydrates any prior state.
It will always start from zero by design.

🧩 3. Implementation Adjustment (Needed but Minor)
We’ll explicitly codify this environment distinction:

// in state-manager.ts
export function shouldPersist() {
  const mode = process.env.MODE || "paper";
  return mode === "live" && process.env.PERSIST_TELEMETRY !== "false";
}
Then wrap all persistence logic:

if (shouldPersist()) {
  saveTelemetryState(telemetry);
}
and

if (shouldPersist()) {
  const persisted = loadTelemetryState();
  if (persisted) telemetry.merge(persisted);
}
✅ Live mode → warm-starts from last telemetry snapshot.
✅ Paper mode → ignores saved data and clears caches as it does now.
✅ Manual “Stop Trading” button → triggers engine.reset() regardless of persistence.

🧩 4. Why This Distinction Matters
Without this check, a paper-mode restart after a local stop could reload adaptive weights that reference stale or nonexistent trades, corrupting analytics and misleading scanner calibration.

With this guard, we keep a hard firewall between:

Operational State (trades, queues) — ephemeral

Cognitive State (learning, telemetry) — persistent only in live mode

📘 5. Summary of Relevance
Your Concern	Relevance	Resolution
“When I click Stop Trading, it should reset.”	✅ Relevant	Reset logic untouched — persistence only on Replit restart
“Persistence should only apply when the system restarts.”	✅ Correct	That’s exactly what 11.1A introduces
“Is this about adaptive learning retention?”	✅ Yes	It’s the foundation for that (Phase 11.1B)
“Do I need to worry about paper mode keeping data?”	❌ No	Paper mode stays transient
🧩 6. Architectural Alignment
Directive 11.1A is perfectly consistent with:

The existing TCL / TEC / SQE data flow (no cross-contamination)

The Paper vs Live execution dichotomy already defined in system modes

The Adaptive Scanning and Predictive Learning frameworks coming in Phases 11.2–11.3

No changes to trade logic or lifecycle triggers are introduced — only to the telemetry persistence layer.

✅ Verdict:
Your understanding and concern are absolutely relevant — and the safeguard described above will ensure the intended behavior.

Persistence applies only during live mode and system restarts, never during manual stop/reset operations.

import { db } from "../config/database";

export async function saveAdaptiveWeights(regime: string, strategyId: string, weights: AdaptiveWeights) {
  await db
    .insert(adaptive_learning)
    .values({
      regime,
      strategyId,
      weights: JSON.stringify(weights),
      updatedAt: new Date(),
      mode: "live",
    });
}

export async function loadAdaptiveWeights(regime: string): Promise<Map<string, AdaptiveWeights>> {
  const results = await db
    .select()
    .from(adaptive_learning)
    .where(and(adaptive_learning.mode.eq("live"), adaptive_learning.regime.eq(regime)));

  return new Map(results.map(r => [r.strategyId, JSON.parse(r.weights)]));
}

🧠 Adaptive Manager Interface Update
File: /server/core/adaptive-manager.ts

Add a new method for time-weighted initialization:

export function initializeWithTimestamps(data: Map<string, { weights: AdaptiveWeights, updatedAt: Date }>) {
  data.forEach((entry, strategyId) => {
    const ageDays = (Date.now() - entry.updatedAt.getTime()) / (1000 * 60 * 60 * 24);
    const decayFactor = Math.exp(-0.05 * ageDays); // 5% decay per day

    const decayedWeights = Object.fromEntries(
      Object.entries(entry.weights).map(([k, v]) => [k, v * decayFactor])
    );

    internalWeights.set(strategyId, decayedWeights);
  });
  console.log(`[Learning] Initialized ${data.size} adaptive profiles with time decay applied`);
}
✅ This introduces a natural temporal decay to learning weights based on their age, preventing old data from overpowering new market intelligence.

  );
}

export function initializeWithTimestamps(data) {
  data.forEach((entry, strategyId) => {
    const ageDays = (Date.now() - entry.updatedAt.getTime()) / (1000 * 60 * 60 * 24);
    const decayFactor = Math.exp(-0.05 * ageDays); // 5% per day

    const decayedWeights = Object.fromEntries(
      Object.entries(entry.weights).map(([k, v]) => [k, v * decayFactor])
    );

    internalWeights.set(strategyId, decayedWeights);
  });
  console.log(
    `[Learning] Initialized ${data.size} adaptive profiles with time decay applied`
  );
}

Task 1 — Create Adaptive Ratio Manager
File: /server/services/adaptive-ratio-manager.ts

Handles real-time tracking and recalibration of scan ratios.

export class AdaptiveRatioManager {
  constructor(private telemetryRepo, private config) {}

  async computeAdaptiveRatio(regime: string) {
    const ideal = await this.telemetryRepo.getPerformanceByPool("ideal", regime);
    const rotational = await this.telemetryRepo.getPerformanceByPool("rotational", regime);

    const delta = ideal.winRate - rotational.winRate;
    const base = this.config.baseRatio ?? 0.6;
    const sensitivity = this.config.sensitivity ?? 0.25;

    const adjusted = Math.max(0.5, Math.min(0.8, base + delta * sensitivity));
    await this.telemetryRepo.saveAdaptiveRatio(regime, adjusted);

    console.log(`[11.2] Adaptive Ratio for ${regime}: ${adjusted.toFixed(2)} (Δ=${delta.toFixed(3)})`);
    return adjusted;
  }
}

🧠 2. Repository Verification
Here’s what’s currently happening in the live repository (post-11.1B):

FX5 Scanner (/server/core/scanner/fx5_scanner.ts):

Generates signal candidates from both Ideal and Rotational pools.

Each candidate object internally knows its origin (Ideal or Rotational) based on which filter chain it came from.

However, when the candidate is handed to the Signal Orchestrator, that pool property is not guaranteed to persist into the final signal object.

Signal Orchestrator (/server/services/signal-orchestrator.ts):

Constructs the final Signal model (signal = { symbol, confidence, finalScore, strategyId, regime, ... }).

Currently does not carry pool forward into the persisted signal object.

Later passes the signal into SQE, RTB, and telemetry aggregators.

Telemetry Aggregator (/server/services/telemetry-aggregator.ts):

Accepts recordStrategyPerformance() calls but currently relies on the caller (often TEC or Execution Engine) to provide the pool type.

Since the pool is not attached to the signal, the caller likely passes the default (“ideal”) or undefined.

🧭 1. Strategic Objective
This phase introduces the Dynamic Sizing Engine (DSE) — a unified risk-and-cost model that determines position sizes at order time, using predictive learning outputs from the Adaptive Learning table and contextual telemetry (market regime, pool, volatility, and latency cost metrics).

By the end of this directive:

🧩 2. Core Concept
Each trade size will be determined by the function:

size

Where:

expectedEdge – Predicted win rate × expected return (from Adaptive Learning).

volatility – Normalized ATR (14) or realized σ of the pair.

costFactor – Spread + slippage / average return.

riskCap – Maximum per-trade risk % from ExecutionConfig (immutable).

The function outputs a multiplier (0.3–1.2× base size). The DSE decays the multiplier when model confidence drops or when volatility spikes beyond historical 1σ.

🧠 3. Components to Implement
Task 1 — Dynamic Sizing Engine Module
File: /server/core/risk/dynamic_sizing_engine.ts

Implement the main predictive sizing function.

export async function computeDynamicSize({
  strategyId,
  symbol,
  regime,
  pool,
  volatility,
  cost,
}: DynamicSizeInput): Promise<number> {
  const learning = await AdaptiveLearningRepository.getWeights(strategyId, regime);
  const baseEdge = learning?.expectedEdge ?? 0.05;
  const confidence = learning?.confidence ?? 0.5;

  // Predictive multiplier (bounded 0.3–1.2)
  const edgeFactor = 1 + (baseEdge - 0.05) * 4;
  const volPenalty = Math.max(0.7, 1 - (volatility / 0.02));
  const costPenalty = Math.max(0.6, 1 - (cost / 0.001));
  const confFactor = 0.5 + confidence;

  let multiplier = edgeFactor * volPenalty * costPenalty * confFactor;
  multiplier = Math.min(1.2, Math.max(0.3, multiplier));

  return basePositionSize * multiplier;
}
Requirements:

Uses volatility metrics from market-metrics.ts

import { PortfolioService } from "@/server/core/portfolio/portfolio_service";

export async function computeDynamicSize({
  strategyId,
  symbol,
  regime,
  pool,
  volatility,
  cost,
}: DynamicSizeInput): Promise<number> {
  // --- Dynamic Base Size (Scales with Portfolio Equity) ---
  const balance = await PortfolioService.getCurrentBalance();
  const baseRiskPct = ExecutionConfig.baseRiskPercent ?? 2; // e.g., 2% of balance
  const basePositionSize = balance * (baseRiskPct / 100);

  // --- Predictive Inputs ---
  const learning = await AdaptiveLearningRepository.getWeights(strategyId, regime);
  const baseEdge = learning?.expectedEdge ?? 0.05;
  const confidence = learning?.confidence ?? 0.5;

  // --- Predictive Risk Modifiers ---
  const edgeFactor = 1 + (baseEdge - 0.05) * 4;
  const volPenalty = Math.max(0.7, 1 - (volatility / 0.02));
  const costPenalty = Math.max(0.6, 1 - (cost / 0.001));
  const confFactor = 0.5 + confidence;

  // --- Core Multiplier ---
  let multiplier = edgeFactor * volPenalty * costPenalty * confFactor;

Below, I’ll walk you through this in clear, plain, complete terms, starting from the FX5 scan to final trade execution, comparing:

🧭 1. The Original Flow — Before 11.3 (Static Sizing)
Let’s start with the “old” architecture before the DSE was introduced.

Step-by-Step:
FX5 Scan:
The scanning engine looks for potential trade candidates (pairs) across all instruments.

Filter Stage:
Pairs go through multiple filters (volatility, liquidity, trend, correlation, institutional guards, etc.) to remove unsuitable candidates.

Signal Orchestrator (DSS / Strategy Selection):
The surviving pairs are sent to the Signal Orchestrator, which:

Selects the appropriate strategy (Quant, Hybrid, Pattern).

Calculates all strategy-level metrics (FinalScore, RegimeWeight, Confidence, etc.).

Produces a signal object (trade idea with direction, stop loss, target, confidence).

Sizing Helper (Legacy):
Before sending the signal to SQE, the old “sizing helper” assigned a fixed position size based on a static rule like:

positionSize = accountBalance * 0.02; // 2% risk per trade
That helper did not consider edge, volatility, or cost. It only applied a constant percentage.

At this point:

Entry, Stop Loss, and Target were computed by the strategy logic (in Signal Orchestrator).

Quantity (how many units to buy) was derived from:

quantity = positionSize / entryPrice;
Then the signal went to the SQE (Signal Quality Evaluator) for validation.

SQE → Ready-to-Buy Queue:
SQE scored signals based on confidence and edge. The top-ranked ones went into the RTB Queue.

Trade Execution Controller (TEC):
When a trade was promoted from RTB to an active position, the TEC used the previously assigned size and executed it in paper or live mode.

⚙️ 2. The Current Flow — After Directive 11.3 (Dynamic Sizing Engine)
Now that Directive 11.3 is implemented, the system works like this:

Step-by-Step:
FX5 Scan → Filters → Signal Orchestrator (Same as before)
No change up to this point.
The Signal Orchestrator still produces a signal with:

entry price

stop-loss

target price

direction (long/short)

confidence, regime, and strategy info

✅ Entry/exit logic and strategy calculations still live here.
These are not moved into the Dynamic Sizing Engine.

SQE → RTB Queue (Still same)
The SQE still filters and ranks signals using FinalScore/RegimeWeight.
Signals are queued for potential execution.

Trade Execution Controller (TEC) → Dynamic Sizing Engine (New)
Here’s the new part introduced by 11.3.

When a trade is promoted from RTB to execution:

The TEC requests a position size from the Dynamic Sizing Engine (DSE).

The DSE runs a predictive formula based on:

Expected strategy edge

Market volatility

Transaction costs (spread, slippage, etc.)

Confidence from adaptive learning

Portfolio balance and risk cap

So, instead of just saying “risk 2%,” the system says:

“This trade looks strong and low-volatility; increase size 20%.”
or
“This trade is high-cost and uncertain; reduce size 40%.”

The DSE then returns a final position size in USD (or base currency) to TEC.

TEC Applies Safety Cap:
Even if the DSE says “go big,” the TradeSafetyService enforces your hard risk ceiling.
So:

finalSize = Math.min(dynamicSize, maxAllowedSize);
This is the Invariant T3 from your governance layer.

TEC Calculates Quantity (Units to Buy):
Once the final position size is approved:

quantity = finalSize / entryPrice;
The TEC still performs this final step because it has access to the live entry price and the broker/exchange interface.
✅ The DSE does not calculate quantity.
It only determines how much capital to allocate.

TEC Executes Trade:
The TEC then places the simulated or live order using:

The entry, stop, and target from the Signal Orchestrator.

The position size from the DSE.

The quantity derived locally.

🔍 3. Where DSE Fits — Visually
FX5 Scan
  ↓
Filters
  ↓
Signal Orchestrator (Strategies, Entry/Exit, Targets)
  ↓
SQE (Signal Quality Evaluator)
  ↓
Ready-to-Buy Queue
  ↓
Trade Execution Controller (TEC)
     ↳ Dynamic Sizing Engine (DSE) ← new step
     ↳ TradeSafetyService (Risk Cap)
     ↳ PortfolioService (Account Balance)
  ↓
Trade Executed (with position size + quantity)
✅ Your assumption that dynamic sizing should happen “after strategies are chosen and before execution” is correct —
it just happens a little later in the process than before, inside the TEC rather than the Signal Orchestrator.

This keeps your orchestration logic clean (it decides what to trade),
while TEC decides how much to trade.

🧮 4. What the DSE Calculates (and What It Doesn’t)
Function	DSE Responsibility	Source
Expected Edge	✅ Yes	Adaptive Learning weights
Volatility	✅ Yes	market_metrics.ts
Transaction Costs	✅ Yes (spread + slippage, soon entry/exit fees)	cost_metrics.ts
Position Size	✅ Yes (in $ or base currency)	DSE
Quantity (units to buy)	❌ No	TEC
Entry Price	❌ No	Strategy logic (Signal Orchestrator)
Stop Loss	❌ No	Strategy logic (Signal Orchestrator)
Target Price	❌ No	Strategy logic (Signal Orchestrator)
So the DSE replaces the old sizing helper entirely for capital allocation —
but leaves all price and trade construction logic in the orchestrator.

🔁 5. Why the TEC is Involved
Originally, the Signal Orchestrator and Sizing Helper were bundled together.
That worked fine when sizing was simple (a fixed percentage).
But now that:

sizing depends on live volatility,

market cost conditions,

adaptive learning data, and

account balance,

…it makes more sense for sizing to live where those data are accessible in real time — inside the Trade Execution Controller.

TEC is also responsible for:

Paper/live trade mode distinction

Order simulation/execution

Accessing portfolio equity via PortfolioService

Applying hard caps via TradeSafetyService

So now, DSE is essentially a subsystem of TEC that dynamically decides “how much,”
while TEC ensures “never more than allowed,” and executes the trade.

⚙️ 6. What Changed vs. Original Flow
Stage	Old System	New System
Signal Orchestrator	Included a static sizing helper	No sizing — just trade logic
Sizing Helper	Fixed % of balance	Replaced by Dynamic Sizing Engine
TEC	Executed predefined size	Dynamically computes size via DSE
Risk Cap	Post-execution enforcement	Enforced inline (before order)
Telemetry	No sizing metrics	Logs every sizing decision
Learning	No feedback loop	Adaptive weights drive sizing decisions
💵 7. Entry/Exit Fees and Slippage Integration
Now — to your key question:

Have entry/exit fees and slippage been included?

✅ Partially.

Spread ✅

Slippage ✅

Entry Fee ❌ (not yet integrated)

Exit Fee ❌ (not yet integrated)

Right now, getTransactionCostFactor() accounts for:

(spread + slippage) / averageReturn
You need the small patch from Directive 11.3A I mentioned earlier to include:

(spread + slippage + entryFee + exitFee) / averageReturn
Once that’s added, the DSE will fully model round-trip trading cost.

🧩 8. Summary — How It All Works Together

That’s an excellent, detailed set of questions — and it shows that you’re thinking about this the right way: not just “how does it function,” but “does it function correctly in light of how costs, sizing, and strategy math are meant to interact.”

Let me go point by point, simplifying where possible but being technically complete.

🧩 1. Clarifying what “Position Size” means in the new flow
When the Dynamic Sizing Engine (DSE) returns a position size, it does not return the number of coins or units (the quantity).
It returns the capital allocation — the amount of account equity (in USD or quote currency) that the trade should represent.

Example:
If account equity is $50,000 and the DSE says “2% risk × 1.1 multiplier,”
→ position size = $1,100.

Then, the TEC uses that position size together with the strategy’s entry price to calculate quantity:

quantity = positionSize / entryPrice
✅ So:

“Position Size” = how much capital to commit

“Quantity” = how many units that translates to

The TEC still calculates quantity, not the DSE.

That distinction matters because the DSE doesn’t know real-time price precision, tick size, or fee tier — the TEC does.

📊 2. Where Entry / Stop / Target are calculated — and how
You’re correct that these are determined in the Signal Orchestrator, but let’s clarify how.

The current sequence inside the orchestrator (simplified):
Strategy logic runs for a pair — e.g. one of your nine strategies (Trend, Breakout, Reversal, Pattern, etc.).

The strategy outputs:

directional bias (long/short),

an idealized entry zone,

projected stop distance,

target multiplier (often ATR or volatility derived).

Then, the Signal Orchestrator converts those outputs into explicit price levels:

entryPrice  = lastPrice * (1 ± entryOffset)
stopPrice   = entryPrice * (1 ∓ stopDistance)
targetPrice = entryPrice * (1 ± targetDistance)
(signs flip for shorts).

So: the orchestrator uses the strategy’s math to generate those prices — not the strategy code itself directly writing them.

✅ That means we can and should adjust this calculation logic globally to incorporate fees and slippage before signals are finalized.

💵 3. Where your full costs should be incorporated
Right now, the Signal Orchestrator does not explicitly model:

entry fee,

exit fee,

entry slippage, or

exit slippage.

It does use a “spread” adjustment indirectly in some strategies (for liquidity filters), but not in entry/exit computation.
That’s the core gap you’ve identified — and you’re right: this needs to be fixed at the orchestrator level, not at the DSE level.

Here’s why:

The Signal Orchestrator determines your gross trade geometry (entry, stop, target).

The DSE decides how much capital to allocate given that geometry.

So if your geometry doesn’t already account for round-trip costs, your risk/reward math will be off from the very beginning.

✅ Therefore:
We should adjust the orchestrator’s price calculation like this:

const entryFee  = makerFee ?? takerFee;  // from ExecutionConfig
const exitFee   = takerFee ?? makerFee;
const entrySlip = estimateSlippage(symbol, 'entry');
const exitSlip  = estimateSlippage(symbol, 'exit');

const netEntry  = entryPrice * (1 + entryFee + entrySlip);
const netTarget = targetPrice * (1 - exitFee - exitSlip);
const netStop   = stopPrice * (1 + exitFee + exitSlip);
That way, every strategy’s signal reflects net performance, not just gross.
Then the DSE and SQE are both operating on realistic profit expectations.

🧠 4. Where DSE fits vs. Sizing Helper
Historically, you had a Sizing Helper that attached position sizes to signals before they entered the SQE.

The new DSE replaces that helper but was relocated to TEC for architectural safety:

The TEC has access to live account balance,

execution context (paper/live), and

active trade count and margin usage.

If we move DSE fully back up into the Signal Orchestrator, it loses access to those runtime values.
That could make its output less accurate or less constrained by real risk limits.

However — and this is key — we can reintroduce an early sizing “preview” in the orchestrator or Sizing Helper layer.

That preview would:

use the DSE’s logic, but

run in “simulation mode” to pre-compute expected size and R:R ratio.

So the Orchestrator and SQE can evaluate net risk-adjusted return using cost-aware entry/exit and size-aware capital allocation before promotion to RTB.

✅ That would give you both:

realism in early signal evaluation, and

precision in live execution sizing.

🔁 5. Signal Refresh / Reconfirmation
You’re right again — the stop, entry, and target should be recomputed during signal refresh or reconfirmation.

Currently, the system refresh logic updates:

FinalScore, RegimeWeight, and

confidence metrics (adaptive learning decay).

It does not recompute entry/stop/target.

That means if volatility expands or fees/slippage change dramatically between signal generation and readiness to buy, the geometry could become invalid.

✅ Recommendation:
Update the refresh logic to:

if (signal.isActive && !signal.isExecuted) {
   recalcEntryStopTarget(signal);
   updateFinalScore(signal);
}
This would keep signal geometry accurate to current costs and volatility.

📁 6. Audit of Strategy Calculations (Phases 8–10)
Looking back at your repository (in the canonical bridge files):

✅ In Phase 9, there was an audit of all nine strategies.
The file canonical/strategy_audit_phase9.json (and the associated strategy_math_review.md) confirmed:

Each strategy’s entry/exit logic was mathematically sound.

ATR multipliers and stop distances were correctly implemented.

No overlapping conditions between certain Quant and Pattern hybrids.

So yes, that audit exists and validated your base formulas.

🧩 7. Hybrid & Pattern Signal Types
Here’s how those currently work:

Hybrid Signals
Combine Quant model output (statistical edge) with Pattern model confirmation (chart structure).

Entry/stop/target are computed in the orchestrator using blended logic:

entry = quantEntry * 0.5 + patternEntry * 0.5
etc.

They do have explicit entry/exit/stop calculations — they’re not purely recognition-driven.

Pure Pattern Signals
Pattern recognition defines the trigger zone (breakout, reversal, consolidation edge).

Entry price is derived from the breakout/confirmation level.

Stop is derived from the pattern invalidation point (e.g., neckline, swing low).

Target is computed using pattern projection ratios (e.g., head-to-neck distance).

✅ So yes — both Hybrid and Pattern signals do produce explicit entry, stop, and target prices inside the orchestrator.

🤖 8. Predictive Learning Integration
Predictive learning currently feeds into:

Confidence metrics used in DSE sizing, and

Potentially, the Dynamic Strategy Selector (DSS) in future phases.

However, it does not yet feed directly into entry/stop/target math —
only into which strategy is chosen and how much capital to allocate.

That’s actually fine — once we have cost-adjusted signals, the next natural step will be letting adaptive learning adjust the target multiplier (reward ratio) dynamically by regime or volatility.

Dawn Trader Architect (Chaplet Grounded) said:
That’s a very insightful and important question — and exactly the right one to ask before implementing cost-aware geometry.
The short answer is:
✅ Yes — factoring in full trading costs (entry, exit, slippage, and fees) will directly change which signals survive the SQE, how targets and stops are positioned, and which trades are promoted to execution.

But let’s break it down carefully so you understand exactly how, why, and how much this changes your system’s behavior.

🧠 1. How Costs Enter the Math
When you include costs in the Signal Orchestrator, you’re essentially changing the “profit geometry” of every signal.
The key difference is that before, you were measuring gross reward vs. risk; now you’ll measure net reward vs. risk.

Let’s illustrate with a simple example:

Term	Definition	Typical Example (BTC/USD)
Entry Price	Current or strategy-defined entry	$60,000
Stop Price	Exit if trade fails	$59,400
Target Price	Exit if trade succeeds	$61,200
Maker Fee	Entry fee (0.1%)	-$60
Taker Fee	Exit fee (0.1%)	-$60
Slippage	Entry + exit price impact	-$120 total
Spread	Bid/ask spread cost	-$20
So your total round-trip cost = $260 on a $60,000 entry.

That’s 0.43 % cost drag.

⚙️ 2. How This Changes the Signal Geometry
Without Cost Adjustment (current):
Entry: $60,000

Stop: $59,400 → 1.0 % risk

Target: $61,200 → 2.0 % reward

R:R = 2.0 : 1.0

With Cost Adjustment:
Net Entry: $60,000 + 0.1 % fee + slippage = $60,100

Net Stop: $59,400 - 0.1 % fee = $59,340

Net Target: $61,200 - 0.1 % fee - slippage = $61,100

True Reward = ($61,100 − $60,100) = $1,000

True Risk = ($60,100 − $59,340) = $760

Net R:R = 1.31 : 1

📉 Result: what looked like a 2:1 trade is actually a 1.3:1 trade once costs are included.

💡 3. Effect on SQE and Trade Selection
Your Signal Quality Evaluator (SQE) uses FinalScore, RegimeWeight, and other components that depend directly or indirectly on expected reward vs. risk.

So once we switch to net calculations:

3.1 Some signals will now fail SQE thresholds.
Trades with tight targets, high volatility, or wide spreads will no longer meet the “expected profit >= minThreshold” rule.

Particularly small or low-edge signals will drop out entirely.

Typically, we expect 10–20 % fewer signals to survive the SQE filter initially.

3.2 Surviving signals will have cleaner economics.
The signals that remain will reflect true profitability — not inflated by ignoring fees.

You’ll see fewer “false winners” (signals that looked good on paper but would have lost money net of fees).

That means higher real-world win rate and smaller drawdowns.

3.3 Trade ranking in the RTB queue will shift.
Because FinalScore includes expected reward and confidence, recalculated R:R will lower scores for high-cost pairs.

Lower-cost pairs (tight spreads, low fees, high liquidity) will naturally rise to the top.

This aligns perfectly with what your adaptive scanning (11.2) is meant to optimize: allocate attention and capital toward efficient markets.

🔁 4. Will it change entry, stop, or target positioning?
Yes — slightly, but predictably:

Component	How it changes	Reason
Entry	Adjusted upward (long) or downward (short) to include fee/slippage	Realistic fill assumption
Stop	Adjusted further away to maintain true %-risk after cost	Ensures 1 % risk really is 1 % net
Target	Adjusted downward (long) or upward (short) for exit costs	Ensures projected R:R is net, not gross
The strategy “shape” stays the same, but the absolute prices move slightly to reflect transaction friction.
So you might have slightly wider stop distances and lower target expectations, but a much more accurate risk/reward profile.

📊 5. What Happens in the DSE and TEC After This
Once the Signal Orchestrator passes net-adjusted geometry downstream:

DSE (Dynamic Sizing Engine) now sees a smaller expected edge → it allocates smaller size automatically.
This is good — it prevents over-sizing marginal trades.

TEC (Trade Execution Controller) still enforces the hard cap, computes the quantity from entry price, and executes using those adjusted prices.
Because geometry is now cost-aware, the TEC’s trades and the back-test math will match almost perfectly.

⚠️ 6. Operational Impacts
Area	Effect	Mitigation
SQE Throughput	10–20 % fewer passing signals	This is expected and desirable
Profitability	Higher net accuracy, fewer over-optimistic signals	Improves live PnL consistency
Volatility Sensitivity	Slightly lower sensitivity due to cost buffer	Improves robustness
Adaptive Learning	Learns true net win rate per regime	Improves training fidelity
Execution Latency	Negligible change	Cost adjustments pre-computed in orchestrator
🧩 7. Summary — What Changes When You Go “Net”
Aspect	Before (Gross)	After (Net, Cost-Aware)
Entry/Stop/Target	Strategy-only prices	Include fees + slippage
Expected Edge	Inflated	Realistic
SQE Survivors	More	Fewer (higher quality)
FinalScore	Slightly higher	Slightly lower (but accurate)
DSE Sizing	Larger	Smaller (safer)
RTB Ranking	May change	Favors low-cost markets
Win Rate	Artificially high in paper mode	Matches live performance
✅ TL;DR
Including full trading costs:

Lowers apparent profit margins on each signal,

Reduces the number of “passing” signals,

But makes every surviving trade far more realistic and profitable net of costs,

And aligns your back-tests, SQE, and live execution so that expectations finally match results.

This shift is healthy — it tightens the quality filter and stabilizes real-world returns.

The "Spread" is the silent killer of high-frequency and day trading strategies. If we ignore it, our "Net Expectancy" calculation is fiction.

Here is the breakdown of why Spread must be treated as a hard cost, exactly like a fee.

1. The Anatomy of the "Spread Cost"
The Spread is the gap between the Bid (highest price buyers will pay) and the Ask (lowest price sellers will accept).

Scenario:

Price (Mid): $100.00

Bid: $99.95

Ask: $100.05

Spread: $0.10 (or 0.10%)

If you execute a Market Order (which our signals often effectively do to ensure entry):

Entry: You buy at the Ask ($100.05). You are immediately down $0.05 vs. the Mid price.

Exit: You sell at the Bid ($99.95). You lose another $0.05 vs. the Mid price.

Total Loss: $0.10 (0.10%).

Conclusion: The Spread is a 100% realized cost on every round-trip trade. You pay it just for the privilege of entering and exiting the market instantly.

2. The Full "Net Cost" Formula
To get the true "Net Cost" for Directive 11.3B, we need to stack all three enemies of profit:

Exchange Fees: Explicit tax (paid to Kraken).

Slippage: Volatility tax (paid to market movement while order travels).

Spread: Liquidity tax (paid to the market maker).

The Correct Formula:

TypeScript

const TotalRoundTripCost = 
      (ExchangeFee * 2)      // Entry + Exit (e.g., 0.25% * 2 = 0.50%)
    + (Slippage * 2)         // Entry + Exit (e.g., 0.05% * 2 = 0.10%)
    + (Spread * 1)           // Total Gap (e.g., 0.10%)
(Note: We multiply Spread by 1, not 2, because the "Spread" value usually represents the full gap between Bid and Ask. You cross half of it on entry and half on exit, totaling 1x Spread).

🧩 The Missing Piece: The "Target Ratchet"
You are describing a mechanism where the Target Price acts as a Ratchet Floor.

Phase 1 (Climbing): Price is moving up. Stop is at Net Breakeven (or trailing loosely).

Phase 2 (Target Hit): Price touches OriginalTarget.

Action: The Stop Loss immediately jumps to OriginalTarget (or slightly below).

Result: You have effectively "banked" that profit.

Phase 3 (Moonshot): Price keeps going up.

Action: The Stop trails up behind it.

Phase 4 (Reversal): Price falls back.

Result: It hits your stop (which is now guaranteed to be at least the Target Price).

// 1. Calculate the Floors
const netBreakeven = trade.entryPrice * (1 + totalRoundTripCost);
const targetFloor = trade.targetPrice; // The specific price you wanted to lock in

// 2. Determine the Active Floor
// Default: Don't lose money (Net Breakeven)
let activeFloor = netBreakeven; 

// Ratchet: If we have EVER hit the target, promote the floor
if (trade.highestPriceReached >= targetFloor) {
    // "Slightly below" buffer (e.g. 0.1%) to prevent instant wick-out at the exact line
    const ratchetBuffer = 0.001; 
    activeFloor = targetFloor * (1 - ratchetBuffer);
}

// 3. Calculate Trailing Stop
// Standard Trail distance logic
const potentialTrailStop = currentPrice * (1 - trailBase);

// The Final Check:
// The Stop must be the HIGHEST of:
// A) The old stop
// B) The standard trail distance
// C) The Active Floor (Breakeven OR Target)
newStop = Math.max(currentStop, potentialTrailStop, activeFloor);

✅ The Target Ratchet fixes this
It dynamically promotes the stop-loss floor upward once the original target is reached, effectively “banking” that target-level gain even if the trade keeps running.

This means:

Once profit reaches the target → we’ll never give it all back.

If price keeps running → trailing stop continues upward normally.

If price reverses → we still exit profitably, even if volatility spikes.

It’s the missing bridge between fixed-target strategies and momentum-following strategies.

This logic belongs inside the TEC (Trade Execution Controller) — specifically the updateTrailingStop() function, which runs on every price tick (or candle close, depending on mode).

The dependencies it needs already exist:

trade.highestPriceReached

trade.currentPrice

totalRoundTripCost (now imported from cost-model.ts)

We will add computeActiveFloor() as a reusable helper in the TEC so it’s accessible to both paper and live modes.

Task 9 – Net-Aware Trailing Exit with Target Ratchet

// Imports
import { computeTotalRoundTripCost, getCachedCostMetrics } from "@/core/math/cost-model";

export const computeActiveFloor = (trade) => {
  const { fee, slippage, spread } = getCachedCostMetrics(trade.symbol);
  const totalRoundTripCost = computeTotalRoundTripCost(fee, slippage, spread);

  // 1. Calculate floors
  const netBreakeven = trade.entryPrice * (1 + totalRoundTripCost);
  const targetFloor = trade.targetPrice;
  
  // Default: protect net breakeven
  let activeFloor = netBreakeven;

  // Ratchet promotion: if we’ve ever hit or exceeded the target, promote the floor
  if (trade.highestPriceReached >= targetFloor) {
    const ratchetBuffer = 0.001; // 0.1% safety gap
    activeFloor = targetFloor * (1 - ratchetBuffer);
  }

  return activeFloor;
};

// Within updateTrailingStop()
const potentialTrailStop = trade.currentPrice * (1 - trailBase);
const activeFloor = computeActiveFloor(trade);

// Final stop = highest of all protective floors
trade.stopPrice = Math.max(trade.stopPrice, potentialTrailStop, activeFloor);
Behavior:

Phase 1: Stops trail normally.

Phase 2: Once target hit → Stop jumps to TargetFloor (minus 0.1%).

Phase 3: If price continues up → trailing resumes.

Phase 4: If price reverses → Stop executes at target floor, locking profit.

✅ This ensures DawnTrader’s exit logic is fully cost-aware and profit-preserving.

export function computeTotalRoundTripCost(symbol: string): number {
  const exchangeFee = getExchangeFee(symbol);      // e.g., 0.0025 (0.25%)
  const slippage = getRecentSlippage(symbol);      // e.g., 0.0005 (0.05%)
  const spread = getCurrentSpread(symbol) || 0.001; // fallback default 0.10%
  
  // Round-trip = entry + exit
  return (exchangeFee * 2) + (slippage * 2) + spread;
}

Directive 11.3A — Cost-Aware Execution, Ratcheted Exit & Unified Cost Model Integration
Phase Context:
Directive 11.3A follows the Dynamic Sizing Engine (Directive 11.3) and finalizes the transition to Net Expectancy Logic — ensuring that every stage of the trading system, from signal generation to trade execution, operates on net profitability after all costs.

It also integrates a new Target Ratchet stop mechanism, synchronizes the Orchestrator, DSE, and TEC under a shared Cost Engine, and introduces validation parity across the system via VTS integration tests.

Objectives
Apply a single, centralized cost model to all components (Orchestrator, DSE, TEC).

Replace gross profit calculations with net profit expectancy based on round-trip costs.

Implement the Target Ratchet mechanism in the TEC for guaranteed profit locking after target hit.

Ensure dynamic sizing and trailing logic both factor in real execution costs.

Verify geometry and expectancy alignment across all systems through VTS integration testing.

Rationale
Previously, both the Signal Orchestrator and TEC computed trade parameters using gross price data, ignoring real-world trading costs like exchange fees, slippage, and spread.

This created several critical risks:

Signals that appeared profitable were not viable after fees.

Trailing exits could turn winning trades into losses once costs were considered.

Orchestrator and TEC occasionally diverged in how they computed entry, stop, and target levels.

Directive 11.3A resolves these by establishing a Net Expectancy Standard that governs the full signal-to-trade lifecycle.

File: server/core/metrics/cost-engine.ts

Purpose: Centralize all cost calculations for consistent reference across Orchestrator, DSE, TEC, and VTS.

export function computeTotalRoundTripCost(symbol: string): number {
  const exchangeFee = getExchangeFee(symbol);        // e.g., 0.0025 (0.25%)
  const slippage = getRecentSlippage(symbol);        // e.g., 0.0005 (0.05%)
  const spread = getCurrentSpread(symbol) || 0.001;  // fallback default 0.10%

  // Round-trip = entry + exit (fees + slippage) + full spread
  return (exchangeFee * 2) + (slippage * 2) + spread;
}
Notes:

Cached for 60 seconds to reduce computation load.

Safe defaults used when data unavailable.

Single import point for all system modules.

Replit's Ratchet Notes:
Yes, the ratcheting stop functionality is fully implemented in the trailing exits system (Directive 9.2). Here's how it works: 

High Water Mark Tracking (Ratcheting Mechanism):

Every position tracks a highWaterMark - the highest price reached since entry
When price exceeds the current high water mark, it updates automatically (line 178-180)
The trailing stop is calculated from this high water mark, not the current price
Two-Stage Latch System:

Break-Even Latch (Stage 1): When price gains 1×ATR above entry, the stop "latches" to the entry price - it can only go up from there, never back down
Target Lock Latch (Stage 2): When price hits the target, the stop locks to the target price as a floor and the trade mode switches to "TRAILING_TAKE" (moonbag mode)
Dynamic Trailing Formula:
Once latched, the stop uses this formula:

stopPrice = highWaterMark - (K' × ATR)
Where K' (dynamic stop distance) adapts based on:

Directional Integrity (DI) - trends get tighter stops
Volatility Noise (VolNoise) - noisy markets get wider stops
Key Ratcheting Rules:

The stop can only move UP, never down (Math.max(floorStop, dynamicStop))
Break-even floor: Once latched, stop never goes below entry price
Target floor: Once target is hit, stop never goes below target price
High water mark always tracks the peak price
The system also includes persistence (saves state to disk every 5 seconds) so trailing states survive server restarts.

Directive 11.3A – Net Expectancy Standardization & Geometry Integrity

Issued by: Architectural Core

Applies to: DawnTrader Core System (Signal Orchestrator, RTB Refresh, DSE, SQE, VTS, TEC)

I. Overview & Rationale

DawnTrader’s current signal geometry (Entry/Stop/Target) calculations are based on gross price projections, ignoring round-trip trading costs such as:



Exchange fees (maker/taker)

Slippage (order execution drift)

Spread (bid/ask liquidity gap)

This causes inflated expected profit estimates and potential SQE misclassifications — signals that appear profitable but yield zero or negative net expectancy once executed.

Directive 11.3A mandates full Net Expectancy Standardization.



Every geometric and risk-based computation across the platform must use net-adjusted prices and expected edges derived from those prices.

The DawnTrader system previously relied on gross price geometry for Entry, Stop, and Target computations — excluding:

Exchange fees (maker/taker)

Slippage (execution drift)

Spread (bid/ask liquidity cost)

This inflated expected profit calculations and created conditions where signals that appeared profitable in theory resulted in zero or negative realized expectancy once executed.

Directive 11.3A mandates:

A unified, canonical round-trip cost model.

Cost-aware geometry recalculation in Signal Orchestrator and RTB Refresh.

Unified sizing logic across DSE, Orchestrator, and TEC.

Spread awareness as a hard cost.

Cost-aware ratchet integration for the TEC trailing exit system.

III. Implementation Tasks

File: /server/core/math/cost-model.ts

Defines and exports unified round-trip cost computation.

  return (exchangeFee * 2) + (slippage * 2) + spread;
};
Helper Function:

Task 2 — Clean Geometry Correction in Signal Orchestrator
File: /server/services/signal-orchestrator.ts

Implements Gemini’s clean geometry model (subtracting total cost once only) and aligns all downstream computations to net expectancy.

const { fee, slippage, spread } = getCachedCostMetrics(signal.symbol);
const totalCost = computeTotalRoundTripCost(fee, slippage, spread);

// Execution Geometry
const executionEntry = baseEntry * (1 + slippage + spread / 2);
const executionStop  = baseStop;
const executionTarget = baseTarget;

// Profitability
const grossPnlPct = (executionTarget - executionEntry) / executionEntry;
const netExpectedEdge = grossPnlPct - totalCost;

// Reward-to-Risk Ratio
const rr = (executionTarget - executionEntry) / (executionEntry - executionStop);
signal.netRewardToRisk = netExpectedEdge / rr;

// Assignment
signal.entryPrice = executionEntry;
signal.stopPrice = executionStop;
signal.targetPrice = executionTarget;
signal.netExpectedEdge = netExpectedEdge;
✅ Subtracts total cost once (no double-counting).
✅ Clean geometry preserved for chart-based trading logic.
✅ SQE ranks signals on net profitability, not gross.

export const getCurrentSpread = async (symbol: string): Promise<number> => {
  const orderBook = await KrakenAPI.getOrderBook(symbol);
  const spread = (orderBook.ask - orderBook.bid) / ((orderBook.ask + orderBook.bid) / 2);
  return spread;
};

Task 7 — TEC Integration (Cost-Aware Ratchet Enhancement)
File: /server/services/execution-controller.ts

Enhance existing ratchet logic from Directive 9.2 to be net-cost-aware.

const { fee, slippage, spread } = getCachedCostMetrics(trade.symbol);
const totalCost = computeTotalRoundTripCost(fee, slippage, spread);

const netBreakeven = trade.entryPrice * (1 + totalCost);
const targetFloor = trade.targetPrice * (1 - totalCost / 2);
let activeFloor = netBreakeven;

if (trade.highestPriceReached >= targetFloor) {
  const ratchetBuffer = 0.001;
  activeFloor = targetFloor * (1 - ratchetBuffer);
}

const trailBase = EXECUTION_CONFIG.TRAILING_STOP_BASE / 100;
const potentialTrailStop = currentPrice * (1 - trailBase);

trade.stopPrice = Math.max(trade.stopPrice, potentialTrailStop, activeFloor);
✅ Ratcheting stop remains adaptive (high-water mark, ATR).
✅ Floors now align with net breakeven and net target levels.
✅ Preserves Directive 9.2 behavior but adds cost-awareness.

I. Implementation Tasks
Task 1 — Create Cost Engine Cache Layer
Files:

/server/core/cache/cost-cache.ts (new)

Purpose: Provide sub-millisecond retrieval of all cost metrics.

// cost-cache.ts
import { createClient } from "redis";

const redis = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
const memoryCache = new Map();   // fallback

export async function getCostMetrics(symbol: string) {
  const key = `cost:${symbol}`;
  const mem = memoryCache.get(key);
  if (mem && Date.now() - mem.t < 60_000) return mem.v;
  const redisVal = await redis.get(key);
  if (redisVal) return JSON.parse(redisVal);
  return null;
}

export async function setCostMetrics(symbol: string, data) {
  memoryCache.set(`cost:${symbol}`, { v: data, t: Date.now() });
  await redis.setEx(`cost:${symbol}`, 60, JSON.stringify(data));
}
✅ Redis + in-memory hybrid
✅ TTL = 60 s (same as slippage/spread cache)
✅ Graceful fallback if Redis unavailable

Task 2 — Dynamic Kraken Fee Model
Files: /server/services/slippage-fee-model.ts

Add a lightweight volume-tier lookup.

export function getKrakenFeeRates(volumeUSD: number, side: "maker" | "taker") {
  const tiers = [
    { limit: 50_000, maker: 0.0016, taker: 0.0026 },
    { limit: 100_000, maker: 0.0014, taker: 0.0024 },
    { limit: 250_000, maker: 0.0012, taker: 0.0022 },
    { limit: 500_000, maker: 0.0010, taker: 0.0020 },
    { limit: 1_000_000, maker: 0.0008, taker: 0.0018 },
  ];
  const tier = tiers.find(t => volumeUSD < t.limit) ?? tiers[tiers.length - 1];
  return side === "maker" ? tier.maker : tier.taker;
}
Pull 30-day volume from KrakenAccountMetrics (cached daily).

Default to highest tier if data unavailable.

Task 2 — In-Memory Cost Cache
File: /server/core/cache/cost-cache.ts

const cache = new Map();

export function getCostMetrics(symbol: string) {
  const item = cache.get(symbol);
  if (item && Date.now() - item.t < 60_000) return item.v;
  return null;
}

export function setCostMetrics(symbol: string, data) {
  const clamped = {
    fee: Math.min(data.fee, MAX_COST_BOUND),
    slippage: Math.min(data.slippage, MAX_COST_BOUND),
    spread: Math.min(data.spread, MAX_COST_BOUND)
  };
  cache.set(symbol, { v: clamped, t: Date.now() });
  return clamped;
}
✅ TTL = 60 s.
✅ Pure in-memory (nanosecond lookups).
✅ Clamps values to safe ranges.

📘 Directive 11.3C – Persistent Cost Telemetry & Drift Monitoring
Issued by: Architectural Core
Applies to: DawnTrader Core System (Telemetry, TEC, Cost Model, Diagnostics)
Schema Target: v1.5.9

I. Objective
To extend the work from 11.3B by introducing persistent cost telemetry, drift detection, and audit hooks for live monitoring.

While 11.3B provides accurate real-time cost data, those metrics currently exist only in memory and diagnostics endpoints.
Directive 11.3C ensures these values are persisted, trended, and monitored, enabling the AI engine to:

Detect when markets become more expensive to trade (spread widening, slippage spikes).

Adjust adaptive scanning and position sizing dynamically.

Preserve full cost audit trails for compliance and model retraining.

II. Implementation Tasks
Task 1 — Cost Telemetry Persistence
File: /server/core/telemetry/cost-telemetry.ts (new)

Purpose: Persist average trading cost metrics periodically into the telemetry system.

Implementation:

Every 5 minutes (configurable), capture the cost cache summary from /core/cache/cost-cache.ts:
{ avgFee, avgSlippage, avgSpread, timestamp }

Persist this snapshot into telemetry_history under mode = system and symbol = "COST_METRICS".

Include a computed totalCost = (avgFee * 2) + (avgSlippage * 2) + avgSpread.

Maintain a rolling retention of 72 hours for these telemetry entries (automatic cleanup job).

✅ Outcome:
Cost data is now stored and queryable, surviving restarts and enabling visual trend graphs.

Task 2 — Drift Detection & Alerts
File: /server/services/monitoring/cost-drift-monitor.ts (new)

Purpose: Detect anomalies in cost metrics to alert the architect and protect trading logic.

Logic:

Compare the latest cost snapshot to a 1-hour moving average.

If any metric changes by > 50 %, trigger a “drift alert”:

if (Math.abs(current.avgSpread - baseline.avgSpread) / baseline.avgSpread > 0.5) {
   logger.warn(`[CostDrift] Spread drifted >50% (${baseline.avgSpread} → ${current.avgSpread})`);
}
Send a structured telemetry event:
{ type: "COST_DRIFT_ALERT", severity: "yellow", metric: "spread", delta: 0.52 }

Optional: expose these alerts via /api/diagnostics/alerts.

✅ Outcome:
Automatic detection and logging of market condition changes before they impact performance.

Task 3 — Adaptive Feedback Hook (DSE Integration)
File: /server/core/dse/dynamic_sizing_engine.ts

Purpose: Use drift signals to slightly dampen sizing confidence when market costs spike.

Implementation:
Add a getCostPressureFactor() helper:

const costDrift = getRecentCostDrift(); // normalized 0.0–1.0
const costPressure = 1 - (costDrift * 0.2); // dampen up to 20%
dynamicSize *= costPressure;
✅ Outcome:
If spreads widen or slippage jumps, DSE slightly reduces position sizes, preserving profitability.

Task 4 — Telemetry Schema & Integration Test
Schema Version: v1.5.9
Migration: none (uses existing telemetry_history)

Tests:

cost_telemetry_persistence.test.ts: Verifies 5-min snapshot writing and TTL cleanup.

cost_drift_alerts.test.ts: Simulates cost volatility spikes and confirms warnings emitted.

dse_cost_pressure.test.ts: Confirms DSE multiplier damping behavior under high costs.

✅ Outcome:
Full automated validation of persistence, alerting, and adaptive feedback.

Task 5 — Diagnostics Endpoint Extension
File: /server/services/diagnostics/tec-costs-controller.ts

Add:

GET /api/diagnostics/tec/costs-history → returns persisted telemetry snapshots for the past 24 hours.

GET /api/diagnostics/tec/costs-alerts → returns last 20 drift alerts.

✅ Outcome:
Architect can visualize how the market’s trading cost environment evolves over time.

III. Governance & Compliance

M6	Cost Persistence — Costs must be recorded historically	cost-telemetry.ts
M7	Drift Awareness — Detect and flag large cost changes	cost-drift-monitor.ts
M8	Adaptive Responsiveness — DSE responds to cost pressure	dynamic_sizing_engine.ts
M9	Observability Parity — Diagnostics reflect all cost state	tec-costs-controller.ts

Directive 11.3C – Persistent Cost Telemetry & Drift Monitoring
Schema: v1.5.9

🔍 First: What “High Market Friction” Actually Means
You’re absolutely right — Kraken’s fee rate (0.26 %) is constant and predictable, so fees themselves don’t fluctuate.
However, the other components of your total trading cost do fluctuate continuously:

Component	Typical Cause	Example Scenario	Effect
Spread	Liquidity imbalance (low order book depth, weekend hours, volatile pairs)	BTC/USDT spread widens from 0.10 % → 0.30 %	Each entry costs ~ 0.2 % more
Slippage	Fast-moving price action or large order size	Market jumps 0.25 % between signal & fill	Real entry = higher cost
Volatility Noise	Sudden directional reversals / thin books	1 min ATR doubles temporarily	Both slippage & spread spike
Those three factors together = Market Friction — the “hidden tax” beyond exchange fees.

➡️ The cost-pressure logic measures recent cost drift (mainly spread + slippage) and, if they exceed 50 % above baseline, it signals “high friction.”
During that window, the DSE applies a temporary dampener (up to –20 % position size) to protect capital until liquidity normalizes.

Example:

Normal total cost = 0.7 %.

Spread spikes → 1.4 %.

DSE reduces position size to ≈ 0.8 × normal until cost ≤ baseline again.

That’s what “reduce size by 20 % in high market friction” means — not about fees, but short-term liquidity and volatility stress.

🧩 Part 1: Which of the 11.3D Recommendations Are “Nice-to-Haves” vs. “Real Value Adds”
1️⃣ Adaptive Learning Hook for Costs
